Article Title: A Michigan scientist buried seeds in 20 glass bottles in 1879; 142 years later, some still grew, and the experiment is set to run until 2100
Article Text:
Michigan State University botanist William James Beal buried 20 glass bottles filled with seeds

A question from 1879

Testing the buried seeds

DNA revealed another surprise

Why the experiment matters

The experiment continues

In 1879, Michigan State University botanist William James Beal buried 20 glass bottles filled with seeds and sand in an effort to answer a deceptively simple question: how long could seeds remain dormant in the soil and still grow when conditions became favourable? According to Michigan State University, more than a century later, the experiment was still producing surprises. In 2021, researchers at Michigan State University unearthed one of the remaining bottles, 142 years after it was buried, and found that some of the seeds could still germinate. The discovery offered a rare glimpse into the extraordinary longevity of seeds and showed why Beal’s experiment remains scientifically relevant more than a century after it began. With bottles still underground, the experiment is scheduled to continue through 2100, making it one of the world’s longest-running scientific experiments.Beal designed the experiment to help farmers understand how long unwanted plants could persist in soil. His concern was practical: if weed seeds could remain dormant for decades, simply removing visible weeds would not necessarily prevent them from returning. To investigate, Beal selected 50 freshly collected seeds from each of 23 plant species. He mixed the seeds with sand and divided them among 20 pint-sized glass bottles.The bottles were left uncorked and buried with their openings pointing downward so rainwater could not collect around the seeds. They were placed on a sandy knoll on the Michigan State campus, creating conditions intended to imitate seeds remaining naturally underground.Beal originally planned to excavate a bottle every five years. During the first decades, researchers repeatedly found that some of the buried seeds could still germinate. The schedule was later changed to preserve the remaining bottles for longer. In 1920, the interval between tests was extended to 10 years. By 1980, it had been increased again, this time to 20 years. That decision transformed the project from a relatively short agricultural experiment into a long-term scientific record of seed longevity.When researchers opened a bottle in 2021, 142 years had passed since Beal buried it. Seeds from the Verbascum group germinated, demonstrating that at least some seeds had remained viable for more than a century. The result was particularly striking because most of the other species included in the original experiment had lost their viability within the first 60 years.The 2021 experiment produced another discovery that Beal could never have anticipated. Researchers used modern genetic testing to identify the plants that emerged from the bottle. The analysis confirmed that the seedlings included moth mullein (Verbascum blattaria) and a hybrid between moth mullein and common mullein (Verbascum thapsus). Beal had recorded that he included only common mullein seeds, suggesting that the hybrid resulted from an accidental mix-up when the bottles were originally prepared. The use of DNA sequencing added a modern layer to a study that began long before genetics became a scientific field.The Beal Seed Experiment is more than a historical curiosity. Understanding how long seeds can remain viable can help researchers study persistent weeds, manage land restoration and understand how plant species survive in soil seed banks.This information can be particularly useful when restoring former agricultural land. Seeds left behind in soil can potentially emerge many years after cultivation stops, meaning restoration teams need to understand which species may remain dormant and which are unlikely to persist for long periods.Beal’s original question has still not been completely answered. Researchers cannot simply assume that seeds that failed to germinate are dead; some may remain dormant and require different environmental conditions before they begin growing. Four bottles remain underground. The next bottle is scheduled to be unearthed in 2040, and the final bottles are expected to keep the experiment going until 2100. If seeds germinate again, researchers may consider increasing the interval between future excavations even further.More than 140 years after Beal first buried his bottles, the experiment continues to demonstrate the value of patience in science. What began as an attempt to understand troublesome weeds has become a living record of how long seeds can survive, and a scientific experiment that will outlast generations of researchers.
Article Summary: Michigan State University botanist William James Beal buried 20 glass bottles filled with seeds and sand in 1879. In 2021, researchers at Michigan State University unearthed one of the remaining bottles, 142 years after it was buried, and found that some of the seeds could still germinate. With bottles still underground, the experiment is scheduled to continue through 2100.

Article Title: A 69-year-old North Carolina father spent $800,000 buying 5 acres; he now wants to build 20 tiny homes so adults like his disabled son can have a community of their own
Article Text: Like most parents, Dave Curro, a 69-year-old father, is also worried about the future of his son, especially since he has a developmental disability. But now, he is one step closer to ensuring that his son has a community that supports him and makes his life more comfortable and happier. Four years ago, he dreamt of creating a community for adults with special needs and now, he is working on it.In March, Curro bought five acres near the intersection of Carver Street and Guess Road for the community known as Forest Grove, where he hopes to form 20 tiny homes. In addition, the project plans a community centre with a catering kitchen, meeting space and multi-purpose room.“I don’t want to restrict it to anything specific,” Dave Curro explained. “The people that live [in Forest Grove] are going to dictate what happens in the community centre, not others.” He said possible uses include a sports watch party, dance lessons and cooking classes.On Saturday, his fundraising campaign with a lively festival attracted more than 800 people. The Forest Grove Festival was organised by Curro's non-profit, the Midtown Housing Coalition (MHC) and featured live music, more than 50 vendors, a kids zone, a petting zoo, local food and representatives from Durham Mayor's Committee for Persons with Disabilities.All proceeds from the festival went towards Forest Grove. “I’m old… which makes this [project] more important,” Curro said.Curro's son, Bret, 39, is the inspiration behind the project. Bret has developmental disability, works at a local hotel and lives in his own apartment. Yet he craves living in an environment with a stronger sense of community and support. “I’m excited to have my own place,” he said.Sandy Johnson, an MHC board member and mom of another hopeful resident, said her son Brandon would benefit from those community programs. “This is why I’m doing this, for him. He’ll thrive, have friends and have a community”. While initially MHC planned to collaborate with Habitat for Humanity for the project, it later chose to work with a private builder instead, which will enable the non-profit to maintain ownership of the property. Curro said MHC spent $800,000 to buy the land and hopes to raise a total of $3.8 million to complete the project. He has a lofty goal of beginning construction in six months, and finishing the site in two years.“They are filling a market gap that doesn’t exist,” said Liz, a Durham mother who brought her two young children who are on the autism spectrum. “This means the world to us.”
Article Summary: Dave Curro, a 69-year-old father, is one step closer to creating a community for adults with special needs. He bought five acres near the intersection of Carver Street and Guess Road for the community known as Forest Grove, where he hopes to form 20 tiny homes. In addition, the project plans a community centre with a catering kitchen, meeting space and multi-purpose room.

Article Title: In 2018, Northeastern planned a 55,000-sq-ft expansion on a Massachusetts peninsula; 8 years later, the town won the right to take 12 acres by eminent domain to keep them open
Article Text:
The town of Nahant during a breezy spring day.Photo credit: Canva

A small town, a big university

The spark of conflict

The town’s bold move: eminent domain

Years of legal wrangling

The state’s highest court rules

What the decision means for Nahant

Campus expansion and land use impacts

A broader conversation about coastal land

A small town’s big statement

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the use of eminent domain to preserve open spaces in small towns? Yes, it's essential for community preservation No, it infringes on property rights 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

In 2018, Northeastern University announced plans for a major marine science expansion on Nahant, a small, densely built peninsula northeast of Boston. The proposal included up to 55,000 square feet of new research and teaching space on a 12-acre coastal parcel that many residents viewed as one of the last large open spaces in town. What followed was an eight-year battle over land use, local control and the limits of university growth in a fragile coastal community. In 2026, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court sided with the town, upholding its use of eminent domain to take the 12 acres and preserve them as open space. As reported by Commonwealth Beacon and Mass Legal Resources, the decision marks a rare victory for a small municipality against a major university in a dispute over the future of its shoreline.Nahant is one of the smallest towns in Massachusetts by area, a narrow peninsula connected to the mainland by a single causeway. With limited land, tight zoning and a strong sense of local identity, the town has long been protective of its remaining open spaces, coastal views and residential character.Northeastern University, a large private research institution based in Boston, has been expanding its marine and environmental science programs for years.The university already operates a marine science centre on Nahant, and in 2018 it proposed a significant expansion: up to 55,000 square feet of new buildings on a 12-acre parcel adjacent to its existing facilities. For Northeastern, the site offered direct access to the ocean, room for labs and field stations, and the potential to grow its research footprint.From the start, the proposal divided the community. Supporters argued that the expansion would bring jobs, research prestige and educational opportunities, and that Northeastern’s presence was already a key part of Nahant’s identity. Opponents worried about increased traffic, strain on local infrastructure, loss of open space and the precedent of allowing a powerful institution to shape the town’s future. As plans moved forward, tensions grew. Public meetings drew large crowds. Neighbourhood groups formed. Local officials found themselves caught between respecting the university’s ambitions and responding to residents’ concerns about overdevelopment on a tiny peninsula.In a striking turn, the Town of Nahant decided to use eminent domain to take the 12-acre parcel from Northeastern. The goal was not to build anything, but to prevent construction: the town intended to keep the land as open space, preserving coastal access, views and habitat.Eminent domain, the government’s power to take private property for public use, with compensation, is more commonly associated with highways, utilities or large infrastructure projects. Using it to block a university expansion and preserve open space was unusual, and legally risky. Northeastern challenged the taking, arguing that the town’s action was improper and that the land should remain available for its planned expansion.The case went through the courts for years. The main questions were whether the town’s stated purpose of protecting open space was a valid “public use” under Massachusetts law, whether the taking was done in good faith or mainly to block Northeastern’s project, and how to weigh the university’s property rights and plans against the town’s vision for its limited land. Lower court rulings yielded mixed results, but the core issue was the same: could a small town use eminent domain to stop a large university’s expansion and keep the land undeveloped?In 2026, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court (SJC) ruled in favour of Nahant, as per reports. The court found that the town’s use of eminent domain to acquire the 12 acres for open space preservation was legal and in accordance with state statutes. The justices emphasised that preserving open space, coastal access and natural resources is a recognised public purpose. The town’s actions also fell within its authority, even if the effect was to block Northeastern’s proposed expansion. And, the university would receive just compensation for the land, as required by law, but did not have a right to dictate how the town used its eminent domain power.The ruling did not question the value of Northeastern’s research or its presence in Nahant; it focused instead on the legal scope of the town’s powers and the definition of public use.For Nahant residents who opposed the expansion, the SJC decision was a vindication. The 12-acre parcel can now be permanently protected as open space, with no risk of large-scale development. The town can maintain public access to the shoreline and views; preserve habitat for birds, marine life and other wildlife; and use the land for low-impact recreation, such as walking, birdwatching and educational programs. For many, the case was about more than one parcel. It was about asserting local control against institutional pressure. In a region where universities and developers often hold sway, the ruling sent a message that small communities can still define their own futures.This ruling sends a loud and clear message to schools like Northeastern: owning property doesn’t mean you get to build on it. Local pushback and legal roadblocks can quickly derail massive expansions, particularly in space-starved areas. Expect other towns to take notes. Municipalities will likely double down on aggressive zoning, open-space protections, and even eminent domain to hold off heavy-handed institutional growth. If universities want to avoid brutal, expensive legal battles, flexing power won't cut it anymore. They’ll need to engage local residents much earlier, approach negotiations in good faith, and make real compromises from day one.The Nahant dispute also fits into a larger conversation about how coastal land is used in a warming, developing region. As sea levels rise and storms intensify, preserving open space, wetlands and natural buffers becomes increasingly important for flood protection and ecosystem health. At the same time, demand for waterfront property, for housing, research, recreation and industry, continues to grow. The 12-acre parcel on Nahant is small in absolute terms, but symbolic: a test of whether communities can prioritise long-term resilience and public access over immediate development gains. The SJC’s decision suggests that, at least in Massachusetts, the law can support that choice.What comes nextWith the legal battle resolved, the focus now shifts to the land itself. The town will need to: finalise compensation to Northeastern for the taken property; develop a management plan for the open space, balancing access, conservation and maintenance; and engage residents in shaping how the parcel is used, trails, signage, habitat protection and possible educational partnerships with local schools or institutions. For Northeastern, the decision means rethinking its expansion plans on the peninsula. The university may look to other sites, scale back its ambitions in Nahant, or seek collaborative arrangements with the town that fit within the new reality.In the end, the Nahant case is about power, place and identity. A small coastal town, outnumbered in resources and influence, used the law to protect a piece of its landscape from a major university’s growth plans. Eight years after Northeastern first proposed its 55,000-square-foot expansion, the town has won the right to keep 12 acres open, ensuring that at least this corner of the peninsula will remain undeveloped for generations to come.
Article Summary: Northeastern University announced plans for a major marine science expansion on Nahant, a small, densely built peninsula northeast of Boston. The proposal included up to 55,000 square feet of new research and teaching space on a 12-acre coastal parcel that many residents viewed as one of the last large open spaces in town. The Town of Nahant decided to use eminent domain to take the land from Northeastern. The goal was not to build anything, but to prevent construction: the town intended to keep the land as open space.

Article Title: In 2024, Utah recycled 15,000 cubic yards of 30-year-old highway concrete on site; enough to fill two Goodyear Blimps became road base for new interchanges
Article Text:
A 30-year-old highway gets a second life

Why recycle concrete on site?

The bigger Bangerter Highway transformation

From old pavement to new infrastructure

What if an old highway could become part of the new one? In Utah, that is exactly what happened. The Utah Department of Transportation (UDOT) recycled around 15,000 cubic yards of concrete from the old Bangerter Highway in 2024, crushing it on site and reusing it as road base for new highway interchanges. The amount of concrete was roughly equivalent to the volume of two Goodyear Blimps, according to UDOT. Rather than sending the decades-old pavement away as construction waste, crews processed it where it was removed, reducing the number of truck journeys needed to transport the material.The concrete came from sections of Bangerter Highway that had been in place for about three decades. As part of a major upgrade, crews needed to remove portions of the old roadway to make way for new freeway-style interchanges. Instead of treating the demolished pavement as waste, UDOT turned it into raw material for the replacement infrastructure.The recycling process took place over roughly five months. Heavy equipment first broke the existing concrete into manageable pieces. The material was then fed into a large crushing machine, where it was reduced to smaller fragments. A magnet inside the crusher separated the steel reinforcing bars, or rebar, from the concrete.The recovered metal was also recycled. The crushed concrete was subsequently processed into road base, the structural layer placed beneath pavement and other roadway surfaces. In effect, part of the old Bangerter Highway became the foundation for its replacement.Construction projects can generate enormous quantities of material that must otherwise be hauled away. Moving that material requires repeated truck trips, adding transportation costs, traffic and fuel consumption.By crushing and reusing the concrete at the construction site, UDOT avoided transporting thousands of cubic yards of material elsewhere. The agency said the approach was intended in part to reduce truck trips around the project area.The project also demonstrates how demolished infrastructure can become a resource rather than simply entering the waste stream. Concrete and asphalt are among the major materials used in road construction that can be recovered and reused, although the exact recycling process depends on the material and project.The concrete recycling was part of a much larger effort to transform Bangerter Highway, a major north-south route through Salt Lake Valley. For more than a decade, UDOT has been working to replace traffic-signal-controlled intersections along the highway with freeway-style interchanges. In 2024, four interchanges were under construction at 13400 South, 9800 South, 4700 South and 2700 West. The overall programme was valued at about $415.3 million.Bangerter Highway carried roughly 60,000 vehicles a day, making the corridor particularly important to commuters and other travellers in the rapidly growing western part of the Salt Lake Valley. The interchange projects were designed to eliminate additional traffic lights, allowing vehicles to move through the corridor with fewer stops while improving the highway’s capacity and safety. And there was another unusual detail to the construction: some of the material being used to build that future highway had already spent decades serving the same road.The idea is simple but striking: break down the old road, separate what can be recovered, process it and put it back into the new one. The 15,000 cubic yards of concrete recycled at the 4700 South project therefore did not simply disappear when the old pavement was demolished. Much of it was given another role, this time beneath the infrastructure being built to replace it. It is a small example of a larger shift in construction: sometimes, the material needed to build the next road is already sitting underneath the one being torn down.
Article Summary: Utah Department of Transportation recycled around 15,000 cubic yards of concrete from the old Bangerter Highway in 2024. The amount of concrete was roughly equivalent to the volume of two Goodyear Blimps. The concrete was crushed on site and reusing it as road base for new highway interchanges.

Article Title: Scientists used fossil wings, lasers and AI to recreate the calls of insects from 165 million years ago; some Jurassic species were already communicating above human hearing
Article Text:
The research focused on nine extinct insect species related to modern crickets and katydids.

How Jurassic insects communicated

The team studied 20 fossil specimens found in Inner Mongolia, China.

Lasers helped reconstruct calls

Calls above human hearing

For 165 million years, the sounds made by insects living alongside dinosaurs were lost to time. Scientists have now recreated some of those calls using fossilised wings, studies of living insects, computer modelling and artificial intelligence.According to Smithsonian Magazine, the research focused on nine extinct insect species related to modern crickets and katydids. The team studied 20 fossil specimens found in Inner Mongolia, China. The fossils preserved important details of the insects’ wings, including structures that were used to produce sound.Researchers say the results offer the best evidence-based approximation so far of what part of a Jurassic forest may have sounded like. Their work was published on August 25 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , along with audio samples of the reconstructed calls.The work also revealed something unexpected. One of the insects, Sigmaboilus peregrinus, appears to have produced sounds between 20 and 22 kilohertz. That is at or above the upper limit of human hearing and means some Jurassic insects may already have been using ultrasonic communication.Unlike humans, crickets, grasshoppers and katydids do not use vocal cords to produce their familiar calls. They use a process called stridulation, which involves rubbing body parts with ridged surfaces against each other.In modern grasshoppers and katydids, a leg can be dragged across a wing. Crickets usually move one wing across the other. The Jurassic insects studied by the researchers had similar structures on their wings.One wing had comb-like ridges, while the other had a scraping structure. When the two surfaces moved against each other, the scraper caught the ridges and produced a series of rapid clicks. These clicks blended together into a continuous chirp.The exact structure of the wings affected the sound. The number and spacing of the ridges, along with the size of the area that vibrated, helped determine the pitch and rhythm of each call.That made the fossilised wings especially useful to scientists. “The beauty of fossil insects is that they can preserve their instruments and receptors on their tough external skeleton, unlike many other animals,” Edmund Jarzembowski, an associate scientist at London’s Natural History Museum who was not involved in the study, told Smithsonian magazine.The scientists first studied how living insects produce sound. They used high-speed cameras and a technique called laser Doppler vibrometry to measure how modern insects’ wings moved and vibrated during stridulation.Those measurements were then used to build and test a computer model. The model showed how differences in wing structures could affect the sounds produced by the insects.The researchers then created two-dimensional models of the fossilised wings and fed their structural information into the computer model. They also considered the evolutionary relationships between the extinct insects and their living relatives.Machine learning was then used to help predict the patterns of the ancient calls. The process produced nine different reconstructed sounds linked to the nine fossil species.Most of the insects appear to have produced relatively low-frequency calls, similar to those made by modern crickets. Their calls were around five kilohertz. Many were described as “pure tone” sounds, meaning they were mainly made up of one frequency.The result would have been clear, high-pitched chirps rather than the hissing or buzzing sounds people may associate with some insects.The most striking finding came from Sigmaboilus peregrinus. The researchers' reconstruction suggested that it could produce a call between 20 and 22 kilohertz.Humans generally hear sounds from about 20 hertz to 20 kilohertz. Sounds above that range are known as ultrasonic sounds.“The first time we reconstructed the song and saw it was over 20 kilohertz, we were so excited,” Jun-Jie Gu, a professor of entomology at Sichuan Agricultural University, said, as quoted by New York Times.The finding challenges a long-standing explanation for why some insects evolved ultrasonic communication. Scientists have suggested that bats may have driven the development of these high-frequency calls because insects could use them to communicate while avoiding predators.But bats appeared on Earth roughly 100 million years after the end of the Jurassic. That means they could not have been responsible for the development of ultrasonic calls in these much older insects.Gu and his colleagues instead suggest that Jurassic insects may have had other reasons to use higher frequencies. One possibility was avoiding predators such as early mammals and other animals.Another was competition between insects. If many species were calling at the same frequency, their signals could have become difficult to distinguish.Gu said the insects may have wanted to “have their own channels”. He added that “165 million years ago, the insect community may have already had sophisticated acoustic niches- multiple species occupying different frequency bands from low to high”.Researchers say the work could also help scientists reconstruct sounds made by other extinct insects. Jarzembowski suggested that AI could eventually be used to study ancient beetles and ants as well.“Perhaps AI will help us reconstruct other insect songs, too,” he said. “Let’s look more closely at their fossils, as there’s a potential paleo-orchestra to be discovered.”Gu said the research could also help create more scientifically accurate portrayals of the Jurassic. His team worked with the creators of a new Netflix documentary mini-series, “The Dinosaurs”, to add reconstructed insect sounds to its Jurassic scenes.Thomas Land, a zoologist who worked as a researcher on the series, said the insect sounds helped create a more accurate Jurassic setting. “It’s such a small detail,” he said, “but we did it because every choice like that makes the whole much more realistic.”
Article Summary: The research focused on nine extinct insect species related to modern crickets and katydids. The team studied 20 fossil specimens found in Inner Mongolia, China. The fossils preserved important details of the insects’ wings, including structures that were used to produce sound. The exact structure of the wings affected the sound.

Article Title: A 33-year-old entrepreneur paid $2.55 million for a neglected 81-room Arkansas hotel; after moving into the property himself, he is spending another $1.1 million rebuilding it
Article Text:
From side hustle to business

A new project

A luxury escape without the price

Some learn business, others are born with a hunch for it. When it comes to Greg Clark, it seems the latter holds true. At 19, he quit his job, paid his rent and was left with just $20 to his name. Today, he is renovating an 81-room hotel in Eureka Springs with a $1.1 million budget. The project, called Hotel Expedition, focuses on creating unique experiences with amenities like yoga and a fire pit, according to a report by PEOPLE.When Clark quit his job, he went back to live with his mom and began buying and selling used tyres on Craigslist out of her carport. This side hustle eventually grew into a multi-state, multi-location automotive business. However, in 2020, when the pandemic hit, Clark began looking for other avenues that could sustain his family without him having to devote 100-hour work weeks.“I found real estate and ended up falling in love with renovating old homes, but not so much with being a landlord,” the 33-year-old told the outlet. “I then turned to short-term rentals and really enjoyed the hospitality side of this business. I was finally able to combine creating beautiful spaces with the dopamine I get from other people loving these spaces.”This newfound love led to Clark moving from short-term rentals to larger hospitality projects. In late 2025, he bought his first hotel in Montana near Yellowstone National Park. After a complete renovation, it opened in early 2026. Despite the Montana hotel not being profitable, Clark says the experience solidified his passion for the business. “I was hooked for life now, so you could almost say these have turned into midlife crisis passion projects where I want to just push the boundaries of what guests accept as normal in hotels, and let my creativity explode on our canvases,” he said.Now, the entrepreneur is taking up his biggest project yet. An 81-room hotel in Eureka Springs, which he purchased for $2.55 million. He had budgeted another $1.1 million for renovations, including furniture, fixtures and equipment. He’s also living on-site while overseeing the massive renovation, which he hopes to complete in time for a grand opening around Christmas 2026.The Eureka Springs property was built in 1993 as a Holiday Inn Holidome, a style of hotel popular in the 1990s that centred guest rooms around an indoor pool area. According to Clark, the building was constructed by stacking concrete blocks in a pyramid-like structure, meaning each guest room is essentially a 25-by-12-foot concrete block that was craned into place.The project, which Clark has dubbed Hotel Expedition, is part of his larger goal to build a collection of 10 curated hotels over the next seven years. “I was inspired to buy this 81-room hotel the moment I walked the property and set foot inside the pool atrium,” Clark said, adding, “I knew right then and there, if I can just get everything else right with this property, this room will never go out of style.”He was drawn to Eureka Springs, which sits in the heart of the Ozarks, in part because of the growth of northwest Arkansas and the area’s attractions, including its historic landmarks, winding roads and rivers, as well as cave dining restaurants.However, transforming the property according to his vision is not proving to be an easy feat. Among the most pressing issues are a pool and hot tub that were in such a poor condition that they had to be closed to guests, along with a damaged elevator and multiple HVAC systems that need to be replaced. The HVAC work alone requires a special crane and large commercial package units.The lobby is also currently closed because guests cannot easily move through the space, making its completion one of Clark’s top priorities in the coming weeks. And as with any renovation of a building that has gone more than 30 years without proper care, Clark said the project has brought plenty of unexpected surprises.The property has also faced significant deferred maintenance, including issues involving its septic systems and roof. Those unexpected costs, along with HVAC expenses that have climbed into the hundreds of thousands of dollars, have forced Clark to make some difficult decisions about where to spend the renovation budget.“We want to offer a level of amenities that cater to guests who want more out of their travel than just a bed and a warm shower,” he said. That vision includes a spa with an in-house masseuse, morning yoga, bracelet-making classes, movie nights by the pool and s’mores kits for guests to enjoy around the property’s fire pits. The goal is to make guests feel as though they’re staying at an upscale resort without the upscale price tag.Clark expects nightly rates to range from around $110 on a weekday to as much as $380 during an event weekend, depending on the season. In order to understand the hotel's target guest, he has also been travelling around the country and sometimes internationally to study hotels serving a similar audience.To keep things interesting, he is documenting the entire process on TikTok. Initially, he began sharing it to be able to look back on the progress and remember the transformation. But then, his videos went viral, amassing millions of views and hundreds of comments. “I had no idea millions of people would want to follow the journey,” he said. “The response has been very overwhelming and very mind-blowing.”“I hope followers can take away that I’m just an average dude; I’m not a corporation, a team of board members, or some rich trust fund kid,” he adds. “This goal is obtainable for any average, normal American.” One phrase in particular has become a personal mantra for him: “If they can do it, I can do it.”
Article Summary: Greg Clark is renovating an 81-room hotel in Eureka Springs with a $1.1 million budget. The project, called Hotel Expedition, focuses on creating unique experiences with amenities like yoga and a fire pit. The goal is to make guests feel as though they're staying at an upscale resort without the price tag.

Article Title: A ‘devil flower’ with no leaves, no branches, no green part has been discovered in a Thai forest, scientists say its bizarre appearance is hiding an even stranger secret
Article Text:
A flower that doesn’t behave like an ordinary plant

Why does it look so strange?

The discovery expands the range of a rare plant group

Fewer than 50 plants are known

It has no leaves, no branches and no green parts, and spends much of its life concealed beneath fallen leaves on the forest floor. Scientists have now described a bizarre new flowering plant from Thailand, naming it Thismia daemona, the “devil flower”, for its dark, horn-like appearance. Details of the discovery were reported by Pensoft Publishers, while the research paper, Thismia daemona (Thismiaceae), a new species from Thailand supported by morphological and molecular evidence, was published in PhytoKeys and is also indexed on DeepDyve. Found in Thong Pha Phum National Park in western Thailand, the plant belongs to Thismia, a genus of tiny, unusual flowering plants sometimes known as “fairy lanterns”. Unlike ordinary green plants, Thismia daemona contains no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise. Instead, it obtains nutrients through underground fungi, remaining hidden beneath leaf litter for most of its life.The most remarkable thing about the new species is what it lacks. Because Thismia daemona is achlorophyllous, it contains no chlorophyll and therefore cannot photosynthesise. Instead, it relies on underground fungal partners for nutrients, a lifestyle known as mycoheterotrophy.Its roots are described as coral-like, while the plant’s above-ground portion consists largely of its unusual flower emerging from the leaf litter. The species was found growing beneath the shade of lower montane forest, alongside small bamboo, at an elevation of about 950–970 metres.That habitat is significant. Species of Thismia are more commonly associated with humid, lowland rainforest environments. The discovery of T. daemona in a seasonal, mountainous forest at nearly 1,000 metres therefore came as a surprise to the researchers.The flower’s appearance explains its dramatic scientific name. It is predominantly blackish, with reddish-orange, fleshy structures around the outside. At the top is a dome-like structure known as a mitre, crowned by three slender appendages.The combination gives the flower an almost fantastical appearance, more like something from a dark forest tale than a conventional flowering plant. The researchers examined fresh and preserved specimens under a microscope and also conducted molecular analyses using nuclear and mitochondrial genetic markers to establish that the plant represents a distinct species. Their findings place it within Thismia section Geomitra, where it is closely related to Thismia betung-kerihunensis.The find is important beyond the identification of one new species. Before Thismia daemona was described, section Geomitra was known from Peninsular Malaysia, Borneo and Sumatra. Its presence in Thailand extends the known northern range of the entire group. The new species also brings the number of Thismia species recorded in Thailand to 16, according to the research report.The discovery comes with a warning, however. Researchers currently know of just one population, comprising fewer than 50 individuals and occupying an area smaller than a football field. Because of its extremely restricted known distribution and the vulnerability of its habitat, the scientists have assessed Thismia daemona as Critically Endangered under IUCN Red List criteria.Although the plants occur inside a national park, protection on paper does not necessarily eliminate the risks facing such a specialised species. Its tiny population and dependence on particular forest and fungal conditions make it especially vulnerable to changes in its microhabitat. The researchers say conservation will therefore need to involve the surrounding communities as well as formal protection.For now, the discovery of Thismia daemona offers a glimpse into one of the forest’s least visible worlds, a plant that abandoned leaves and sunlight, lives largely out of sight and depends on fungi underground, yet produces one of the most striking flowers botanists have encountered in Thailand.
Article Summary: Thismia daemona has no leaves, no branches and no green parts. Instead, it obtains nutrients through underground fungi, remaining hidden beneath leaf litter for most of its life. The plant belongs to a genus of tiny, unusual flowering plants sometimes known as ‘fairy lanterns’

Article Title: A bigger Africa & a smaller Europe: What changes in new UN-backed world map
Article Text:
164 countries led the Togo-led campaign

Why India backed resolution

(With agency inputs)

The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Friday endorsed a new world map that more accurately reflects Africa’s actual size, marking the culmination of a Togo-led campaign backed by the African Union and various advocacy groups.The UNGA adopted a resolution titled “Correct The Map”, with 164 member states voting in favour. The United States was the only country to vote against the resolution, while six countries — Serbia, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova and Ukraine — abstained.The campaign urged governments and institutions worldwide to move away from the traditional Mercator projection, which has been widely used since the 16th century, and adopt the Equal Earth projection. Advocates and geographers say the Equal Earth map provides a more accurate representation of the relative size and proportions of continents.Under the Mercator projection, Greenland appears roughly comparable in size to Africa, despite being far smaller. The Equal Earth projection, by contrast, depicts continents in more accurate proportions, showing Africa as about 14 times larger than Greenland.However, the resolution does not prohibit the use of the Mercator projection or mandate its replacement.According to a UN report, it simply encourages governments and institutions to consider using the Equal Earth projection instead.“Maps shape our understanding of the world,” Togo’s foreign minister Robert Dussey was quoted by the UN as saying ahead of the vote. “They guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions.”Africa No Filter, one of the leading groups behind the campaign to promote the new map, welcomed the resolution and called for more widespread use of accurate maps.“We want to see accurate maps in schools, textbooks, newsrooms, businesses and on the digital platforms billions of people use every day,” the organisation said.The Mercator projection was developed by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to assist European navigators at sea. However, critics argue that the projection significantly distorts the size of landmasses, making regions closer to the poles, such as North America and Greenland, appear much larger while making Africa and South America appear smaller.On the map, Alaska appears to be roughly the same size as Brazil. In reality, Brazil is nearly five times larger. Alaska is about 1.7 million square kilometres, while Brazil is about 8.5 million square kilometres.Antarctica appears massive at the bottom of a Mercator map, stretching out to look like an enormous continent that dominates the bottom of the world. While it is still large, its visual area is heavily exaggerated compared to landmasses near the middle of the map.Introduced in 2018, the Equal Earth projection takes the Earth’s curvature into account and presents continents in proportions that more closely reflect their actual size. In it, Europe appears to shrink, Brazil balloons, and Greenland dramatically diminishes. Africa appears much larger in comparison.Explaining India's stand, First Secretary at the Permanent Mission of India to the UN, Raghoo Puri, highlighted that Equal Area projections preserve the relative sizes or areas of continental and territorial landmasses.“This can help address distortions in perceived landmass size that arise from projections designed primarily to preserve other geographic characteristics such as shape, direction, or distance. At the same time, different projections serve different cartographic purposes. No single projection is necessarily appropriate for every application.""Therefore, we believe it is important for this resolution to remain technological and methodological-neutral. Our delegation supports the language that encourages accurate cartographic representation while allowing countries, institutions and cartographers to determine which projection is most appropriate for their specific needs,” he added.However, Puri clarified that India’s position is limited to the principle of encouraging Equal Area approaches where the objective is to preserve the relative sizes of continental landmasses.
Article Summary: The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Friday endorsed a new world map that more accurately reflects Africa’s actual size. The UNGA adopted a resolution titled “Correct The Map’, with 164 member states voting in favour. The United States was the only country to vote against the resolution, while six countries abstained.

Article Title: Meet Kiran Reddy, the 18-year-old Georgia teen who became the first Indian American to win Miss Teen USA
Article Text:
Kiran Reddy makes history just weeks after becoming first Indian American to win Miss Georgia Teen USA

Academic background and roots in Georgia

Cultural impact and upcoming international stage

An 18-year-old student from Douglas, Georgia, has made history by becoming the first Indian American to win the national Miss Teen USA crown. Kiran Reddy defeated 50 other contestants during the 44th annual pageant, held at the Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts in Miami, Florida, on 26 August 2026, according to WALB News and Pageant Circle. Reddy, who had earlier become the first Indian American to win the Miss Georgia Teen USA title, also secured Georgia’s first national victory in the pageant’s history. Her win marks a double milestone for diversity and state representation in the long-running beauty contest.Speaking after her victory, Reddy shared her emotions about taking on the prestigious title. "I am so blessed to represent Georgia and the U.S. and be the role model I always needed growing up," Reddy said, as reported by KFI AM 640. The national finals brought together contestants from all 50 states and the District of Columbia. Raquel Olea of Arkansas was named first runner-up, while Elisa Akin of New York, Kiersten Alvarado of Indiana, and Chloe Bella Dietz of Texas completed the top five. The event was hosted by model Sean Michael Rae and former titleholder Noelia Voigt.Last year’s winner, Mailyn Marsh of Missouri, placed the crown on her successor. The judging panel included notable figures such as Kelsey Swanson, a former Miss Rhode Island USA.Before gaining national attention, Reddy achieved academic success in Coffee County, Georgia. She graduated as the valedictorian of Coffee High School in Douglas. After graduating from high school, Reddy enrolled at the University of Georgia, where she is studying biological sciences on a pre-medical track. Her goal of working in healthcare has been an important part of her platform alongside her pageant career. Reddy’s journey in pageantry has taken years of hard work. She entered competitive pageants at the age of 15. She finished as first runner-up at the Miss Georgia Teen USA contest in 2024, followed by a second runner-up finish in 2025. Her path to the national title began in June 2026, when she was appointed Miss Georgia Teen USA through an open casting call organised by the national pageant organisation, according to reports by WALB and Wikipedia.Reddy’s historic victory highlights the growing representation of Indian Americans in US beauty pageants. As the first Indian American teenager to win the national crown, her achievement has attracted attention from community leaders and pageant fans around the world. Her duties as Miss Teen USA will soon include international representation. Reddy is scheduled to represent the United States at the Miss Teen Universe contest in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, in October 2026. This will be the first time the national organisation participates in the global event. Along with international travel and official appearances, Reddy plans to continue her undergraduate pre-med studies at the University of Georgia while carrying out her duties as Miss Teen USA.
Article Summary: Kiran Reddy, 18, is the first Indian American to win the national Miss Teen USA crown. She defeated 50 other contestants during the 44th annual pageant in Miami, Florida, on 26 August 2026. Her win marks a double milestone for diversity and state representation in the long-running beauty contest.

Article Title: Three children dead and a mistrial: What is the Lindsay Clancy case?
Article Text:
Clancy remains charged with three counts of first-degree murder and is being held in a psychiatric hospital

What happened to Lindsay Clancy’s children?

Defence says postpartum psychosis led to killings

Trial ends in deadlock after courtroom drama

What happens to Lindsay Clancy after the mistrial?

The closely watched trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy, accused of killing her three young children, ended in a mistrial on Friday after jurors failed to reach a verdict following seven days of deliberations. The dramatic conclusion came after a five-week trial that focused largely on one question: Was Clancy criminally responsible for the deaths, or was she suffering from severe mental illness at the time?Clancy, 36, has never disputed that she strangled her children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and eight-month-old Callan, at the family’s home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, on January 24, 2023. Her defence argued that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis, suffering from hallucinations and delusions that left her unable to understand the nature of her actions. Prosecutors, however, argued that the killings were intentional and calculated and that Clancy knew what she was doing.Prosecutors allege that on January 24, 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all three of her children at their home south of Boston. After the killings, she jumped from a second-floor window in an apparent suicide attempt.Her husband, Patrick Clancy, had left the house to get food and medication.When he returned, he found the children dead in the basement and Clancy seriously injured outside the house. She suffered severe spinal injuries in the fall and was left paralysed from the waist down. She attended the trial in a wheelchair.Patrick described the last time he saw his son Dawson alive, recalling him sitting on the couch eating chicken nuggets before he left the house. When he returned, the children were dead.A recording of Patrick’s 911 call was played in court, with him screaming, "She killed the kids". Clancy sobbed as the recording was played.Clancy's family members testified that her mental health had deteriorated significantly in the weeks before the killings. Her former mother-in-law Susan Clancy said she was "begging for help", while her mother Paula Musgrove testified that Clancy had told her she was having thoughts of harming her children.Her sister Allison Ozga told the court that Clancy was experiencing suicidal thoughts every day in the month before the killings.The central issue at trial was not whether Clancy killed her children, but whether she was legally responsible for doing so.Her lawyers argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare and severe mental health condition that can involve hallucinations, delusions, mania and depression following childbirth. They pointed to her treatment for mental health problems and the fact that she had checked herself into a psychiatric hospital just days before the deaths.Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse, had also sought help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room and was prescribed more than a dozen medications during her treatment.The defence presented evidence that Clancy had become increasingly paranoid, depressed and suicidal. Her family described her as a loving and nurturing mother who changed dramatically after the birth of her youngest child.Her husband said her "big spiral" began about a month before the children died."She started to lose a lot of weight, and she became very depressed, and she was having a really hard time," he said.But prosecutors presented a different picture. They argued that Clancy deliberately sent Patrick out on errands before killing the children and that her actions showed she understood what she was doing.More than 10 expert witnesses testified during the trial, with psychiatrists and other specialists offering conflicting views about Clancy’s mental state and whether the evidence supported a diagnosis of postpartum psychosis.One prosecution psychiatrist, Jennifer Tufts, testified that Clancy had not shown signs of psychosis during their sessions. She said there were "no serious signs that her safety or anyone else's safety was at risk".The defence challenged her testimony, pointing to medical notes that referred to Clancy's "not hyper, pressured speech". Tufts rejected the interpretation put forward by the defence, saying the "not" applied to both "hyper" and "pressured"."I don't care what it says. I know what I meant," she said.The five-week trial attracted widespread attention, with thousands of people following the proceedings online. Hundreds of women also gathered outside the courthouse in support of Clancy, wearing pink shirts carrying messages including "She Needed Help" and "Peace For Lindsay".The trial itself was marked by several clashes between lawyers and witnesses.Two days before closing arguments, the defence sought a mistrial after prosecutors questioned witnesses about Clancy’s Catholic faith. The judge later instructed jurors to disregard the testimony, calling it an "absolutely inappropriate area of testimony"."It is to be stricken. It is not to be considered. I can't be any more clear of that," Judge William F. Sullivan said.The biggest drama, however, came during jury deliberations.After seven days, the jury remained deadlocked. A note from the jury indicated that one juror was allegedly not following the judge's instructions concerning reasonable doubt. Clancy's lawyer Kevin Reddington asked for the juror to be removed, but Sullivan rejected the request and instead instructed the jury again on the law.On Friday, Sullivan was preparing to declare a mistrial when Reddington made a last-minute appeal to Massachusetts' highest court, seeking to stop the declaration and have the disputed juror removed.The appeal was rejected, and Sullivan formally declared a mistrial.Reddington blamed the deadlock on the juror, saying the other jurors had been "robbed" of the chance to reach a verdict."They know they were robbed by one man, for whatever his agenda was, who stole seven weeks of the life of these other jurors that were so attentive, so beautiful, so wonderful," he said outside the courthouse. "You could see how defeated they were sitting there. I got a funny feeling they would have gone on for another week if they had to. So I hope that guy can sleep well at night."Prosecutors disputed the defence's characterisation of the juror, arguing there was nothing in the jury's notes showing "a lack of impartiality, bias, extraneous influence, or inability to deliberate."The mistrial does not amount to an acquittal, and Clancy remains charged with three counts of first-degree murder.Judge Sullivan has scheduled a hearing for September 29. The defence could ask him to declare Clancy not guilty, although such a move is considered unlikely to succeed.The prosecution could seek a second trial, negotiate a plea deal or, in theory, drop the case. Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said there would be no immediate decision on whether to retry Clancy.But Cruz made clear that prosecutors continue to view the case as one involving three murdered children."This case was about Lindsay Clancy and what she did … the cruel and calculated killing of three innocents," Cruz said shortly after court ended on Friday. He later continued, "Children were murdered and it’s our job to seek justice."A retrial would mean another lengthy and emotionally difficult process for Clancy's family and for Patrick Clancy, who has already testified about the deaths of his children.
Article Summary: Clancy, 36, has never disputed that she strangled her children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and eight-month-old Callan, at the family’s home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, on January 24, 2023. Her defence argued that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis, suffering from hallucinations and delusions that left her unable to understand the nature of her actions. Prosecutors said the killings were intentional and calculated and that Clancy knew what she was doing.

Article Title: 'That sound follows me': Guests describe chilling scenes after US bombing tore through Iran wedding
Article Text:
Guests recall horror of US bombing that killed five in Iran

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think media coverage of conflicts effectively highlights the impact on civilian lives? Yes, it raises awareness No, it often downplays civilian suffering 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Women and children had gathered at a family home in Kuhestak, a coastal town in southern Iran, waiting for the bride and groom to arrive for a wedding celebration when an explosion tore through the house on Tuesday evening, killing four people and injuring dozens.Days after the incident, wedding guests recalled the chaos and fear that followed the blast. The explosion came during a US bombardment of southern Iran. Four people were killed at the scene, while a fifth victim, a 22-year-old woman who was critically wounded, died in hospital two days later, bringing the death toll to five, according to Drop Site News. At least 60 people were wounded.Speaking to US media outlet Drop Site News, wedding guest Zeinab Mallahi, who was at the house when the blast struck, recalled the moment the building collapsed.“I still hear the voices of the women who were ululating, and then suddenly the roof of the living room and the walls came down on us,” Mallahi told Drop Site News. “That sound follows me from night into day and from day into night.”According to AP, roughly 150 women were gathered at the house, while men attending the wedding were celebrating separately in another building about 50 metres away. The bride and groom had not yet arrived when the strike hit the room where the women were due to be served dinner.Ali Mallahi told AP that the blast left a gaping hole in the roof, shattered windows and cracked walls. Debris, household appliances and sections of roofing were scattered across the compound.Sasan Zarei, a neighbour who rushed to the scene, told AP: “Most of the injured were kids. The scenes were very heartbreaking.”Mallahi, the bride’s father, told Drop Site News that around 350 people had gathered for the wedding. “I really don’t know what to say,” he said. “This happened in a completely residential area. There were no military facilities around the house.”He said he initially thought a gas cylinder had exploded before hearing further blasts.“For a moment I just froze. I didn’t know what had happened,” Mallahi said. “I asked myself, did they really fire a missile at my house? What happened to my daughter’s wedding? What happened to my guests? My children, my wife, everyone?”US vice president JD Vance said Thursday that the incident was being investigated. “We’re investigating it very fully,” he said, adding that the US “never targets civilians in combat” but that “sometimes things happen”.A Reuters investigation found that the wedding bombing was likely a direct hit by a US munition rather than a ricochet from another target.After the strike, bloody shoes and wedding decorations lay scattered among the rubble, another eyewitness told Reuters, “Kuhestak is destroyed. Four, five, ten houses were destroyed. God help us. ”Mostafa Taheri, a Red Crescent emergency worker, told Drop Site News that multiple wedding guests were still trapped under the rubble when rescuers arrived, while others had been injured by shrapnel.“It was the first time I had encountered such a scene,” Taheri said. “We could hear the wounded screaming. We immediately started finding people, moving the rubble and transferring the injured.”Kuhestak lies about 30 km from Minab, where more than 100 children were killed in a US missile strike on a primary school on February 28, the opening day of the war launched by the US and Israel.
Article Summary: Women and children had gathered at a family home in Kuhestak, a coastal town in southern Iran, waiting for the bride and groom to arrive for a wedding celebration. An explosion tore through the house on Tuesday evening, killing four people and injuring dozens. The explosion came during a US bombardment of southern Iran.

Article Title: Too many allies? Why Netanyahu's far-right partners are hurting him in upcoming Israel polls
Article Text:
Netanyahu’s far-right allies in Israel are posing biggest challenge for him

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing an unusual threat ahead of the October 27 election: divisions within the far-right bloc that support his government.Smotrich’s Religious Zionism and Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power, which ran together in the 2022 elections, have rejected Netanyahu's calls for another merger amid tensions. Meanwhile, smaller parties led by former Likud members and former general Ofer Winter are competing for the same right-wing voters, deepening fragmentation.“When we unite, we win. When we split up, we lose,” Netanyahu told Israel's local media outlet Channel 14, according to AP.Netanyahu currently heads a coalition of religious and ultranationalist parties.Netanyahu’s Likud party on Friday rebuked national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for refusing to run on a joint slate with finance minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party, warning that a divided vote could weaken the coalition’s chances of retaining power.Several smaller parties are competing for the same right-wing electorate, raising the prospect that some could fall below Israel’s electoral threshold and leave their votes without parliamentary representation.Under Israel’s electoral system, parties must secure at least 3.25 per cent of the vote to win representation in the 120-member Knesset. A party that falls below the threshold receives no seats, making fragmentation particularly consequential for Netanyahu’s bloc.The Financial Times reported that Netanyahu has sparred publicly with Ben-Gvir, who rejected a meeting this week to discuss a merger with Smotrich. Ben-Gvir accused the prime minister of an “attempt to weaken” his Jewish Power party.Netanyahu responded by urging Ben-Gvir to “not burn tens of thousands of rightwing votes . . . and crown a leftwing government”, while also telling him to “overcome your personal ego”.Ben-Gvir, however, argues that a merger could cost his party seats. “According to all the polls, a connection between me and Smotrich distances Jewish Strength by 3-4 mandates who won't come to vote, and the right-wing government will fall!” he wrote on X.The dispute has left Netanyahu pressing harder for unity. In a video posted on X, he said Smotrich and Ben-Gvir “must unite. Every time we ran united, we won. When we ran separately, we lost.”“In 1992, the Right had more votes than the Left, like today, but because we were running separately, we got the disaster of Oslo, Arafat, Hamas and recurring catastrophes,” Netanyahu said, referring to the peace process launched through the Oslo Accords.Smotrich appeared more receptive, writing on X, “It's time for unity and responsibility in the national camp.”Netanyahu subsequently invited Ben-Gvir and Smotrich to meet on Sunday, saying, “We must not waste a single vote; we must unite to save the right-wing bloc!”The stakes are high for Netanyahu, whose nearly uninterrupted 17 years in power are being tested in an election shaped by the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, mass protests and wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.The parties have until September 8 to decide whether to merge, withdraw or contest the election separately.
Article Summary: Netanyahu currently heads a coalition of religious and ultranationalist parties. The parties have until September 8 to decide whether to merge, withdraw or contest the election separately. Several smaller parties are competing for the same right-wing electorate, raising the prospect that some could fall below Israel's electoral threshold and leave their votes without parliamentary representation.

Article Title: In the 1920s, radio star Will Rogers built a 186-acre Pacific Palisades ranch; after his widow died in 1944, the property became a California state historic park
Article Text:
Dutch Windmill Chapel, Los Angeles, California, United States. Image credits: Wikipedia

The 31-room Ranch House, built in 1926

Rogers dies in a plane crash with Wiley Post

January 2025: The

Palisades fire

destroys the Ranch House

The park reopens after a ten-month closure

Eames House, Case Study House No. 8, Charles and Ray Eames. Image credits: Wikipedia

Will Rogers started acquiring property in the hills above Santa Monica in the early 1920s, assembling a private 186-acre ranch overlooking the Pacific Ocean in what is now Pacific Palisades; the land would not become a state park until 1944. California State Parks and other secondary sources both describe the property as 186 acres. In the early 1930s, Will Rogers was among the highest-paid actors in Hollywood, and the ranch gave him a place to ride horses and play polo.The centerpiece of the property was a 31-room ranch house, according to California State Parks, where Rogers and his wife, Betty, raised their three children: Will Jr., Mary, and Jim. The National Register of Historic Places lists the house's year of construction as 1926, with a period of significance spanning 1925 to 1949, reflecting the fuller span of Rogers' activity on the land rather than the building alone. That same federal listing records the house's original address as 14253 Sunset Boulevard, the address on file when it joined the Register in 1971; the park's current address is 1501 Will Rogers State Park Road.However, Rogers' career ended on August 15, 1935, when he died in a plane crash with fellow aviator Wiley Post in Alaska. Betty Rogers took possession of the property and continued hosting polo games at the ranch field.She died in 1944, the same year she ensured the 186-acre property would pass into public hands: California State Parks says she wanted the ranch preserved as a memorial to her husband, and the land became Will Rogers State Historic Park, open to the public ever since. The ranch house was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on February 24, 1971.The Palisades Fire ravaged the ranch house in Will Rogers State Historic Park in January 2025. As ICT News explains, the fire completely destroyed the house in the Los Angeles fires of Jan. 8. However, state parks personnel saved several pieces of artwork and personal belongings before the flames engulfed the structure. Jennifer Rogers-Etcheverry, a great-granddaughter of Rogers, indicated that she wanted to get involved in the park's restoration efforts. The park was owned by California State Parks the entire time, but the park itself was closed due to fire, including popular trails like those leading to Inspiration Point, while the damage was being assessed. The regulation-sized polo field within the park, which had hosted polo matches on the very ground Rogers rode across, escaped relatively unscathed from the fire.The park had been closed for ten months to conduct clean-up and assess the extent of damage. According to California State Parks and various other news sources like LAist and OutdoorHub, the park opened its doors to the public again on November 8, 2025, with operating hours set to run from 8 a.m. until sunset, and with limited on-site parking. As per CBS LA, all nine miles of trails in the park were open to the public on that day except the Backbone Trail, the Rivas Canyon and Temescal Trail, and portions of the Inspiration Point Trailhead. Opening day featured guided hikes, historical walks, a polo demonstration, free coffee and ice cream, and lawn games, giving residents their first chance in nearly a year to walk the grounds Rogers once called home.The 31-room ranch house burned down entirely in the fire, leaving nothing except its foundation, while a security fence has been erected around the remains, which comprise two chimneys and portions of the original stonework walks. According to California State Parks, the future of this site would depend on a public outreach program to start in 2026, which would help restore the Will Rogers State Historic Park as a homage to his former ranch residence.

The centerpiece of the property was a 31-room ranch house, where Rogers and his wife, Betty, raised their three children. Article Title: Winston Churchill bought Chartwell as his family home in 1922; 104 years later, visitors can still explore about 80 acres of grounds
Article Text:
Winston Churchill bought Chartwell with 82 rolling Kent acres. Image credits: Wikipedia

An undistinguished farmhouse with a view over the Weald

Philip Tilden's alterations, 1922 to 1924

Financial strain nearly cost Churchill his home

Chartwell Clementine. Image credits: Wikipedia

80 acres open to visitors

In September 1922, Winston Churchill acquired Chartwell, a red-brick farmhouse on about 80 acres (often cited as 82) in the Kent Weald, some 30 miles south of London. Mainly Museums notes that Churchill's purchase came at a personal and professional low point: the year before, in August 1921, his family had mourned the death of his two-year-old daughter, Marigold, and within weeks of completing the sale he would lose his Dundee parliamentary seat in the November 1922 general election. Chartwell went on to serve as his family home for the next four decades, a period the National Trust confirms in its own account of the property.It is not the architecture that convinced Churchill to buy Chartwell. He bought a farmhouse that had tile-hung gables and small and dark windows, one that was largely in a dilapidated condition in the latter half of the nineteenth century. It is the sight of the Weald from the garden side of Chartwell that appealed to him. The Historic Environment Record of Kent County Council, under the official entry for Chartwell Garden, mentions how the location is at the head of a valley, with slopes leading south to distant views of the Kentish landscape and plain of River Eden.To turn the farmhouse into a comfortable family home, Churchill engaged architect Philip Tilden, who worked on the property from 1922 to 1924. According to the Historic Environment Record maintained by Kent County Council, Tilden's alterations included adding an eastward wing, a stepped gable on the south front, and simplifying the west elevation.In the decades that followed, Chartwell proved to be far more than a simple retreat: it became an expensive property to maintain. Churchill faced repeated pressure to sell it, most seriously after the Second World War, when his finances were again under strain. In the words of the International Churchill Society , the property continued to weigh on his finances until a group of his friends and admirers, led by Lord Camrose, bought it in 1946.Churchill passed away in January 1965, after Chartwell had been his home, on and off, for nearly four decades, a stretch that included a serious stroke he suffered in 1953 while serving his second term as prime minister, an episode both the National Trust and the International Churchill Society recount in their histories of the house. Clementine relinquished her claim to the property soon afterward, and on 22 June 1966 the Trust opened the estate to the public, as detailed in the National Trust's own account of Chartwell's history. Garden designer Lanning Roper then advised on the grounds from 1965 to 1980, and Historic England's register entry for Chartwell notes that his work, most concentrated between 1965 and 1968, shaped much of the garden's present-day planting and layout, building on the structural features Churchill had already built himself, including the lakes and the kitchen garden walls.More than a century after Churchill signed the purchase papers, 104 years on from 1922, Chartwell remains open as a National Trust property, as the International Churchill Society's own visitor page confirms. Visitors can explore about 80 acres of grounds, including the hillside gardens the Churchills created, the lakes Churchill built, the walled kitchen garden he helped construct, and an orchard surrounded by wildflower meadow. The interiors still hold items Churchill left behind, such as books and personal memorabilia, along with the largest collection of his paintings, exhibited in the studio he used.
Article Summary: Winston Churchill bought Chartwell, a red-brick farmhouse on about 80 acres (often cited as 82) in the Kent Weald in 1922. Chartwell went on to serve as his family home for the next four decades, a period the National Trust confirms in its own account of the property.

Article Title: Model T founder Henry Ford owned more than 2,000 acres around Fair Lane in 1909; after his death, the Michigan estate became a historic landmark
Article Text:
Fair Lane from the Rouge River side. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The story from 2,000 acres to a private estate

The mansion was surrounded by farms, orchards and technology

Fair Lane from the Rouge River side. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The Ford family home is now recognised as a National Historic Landmark

In the years after the turn of the 20th century, Henry Ford began assembling land around Dearborn, Michigan. The National Park Service’s historical nomination records say that Ford had acquired more than 2,000 acres by 1909; this included farmland, woodland and a property along the Rouge River Eventually, the land turned into the setting for Fair Lane, the home he shared with his wife, Clara, a carefully designed estate which combined architecture, gardens, agriculture and Ford’s interest in technology. In 1966, 19 yearsafter Ford’s death, Fair Lane was recognised as a National Historic Landmark.In 1903, Henry Ford organised the Ford Motor Company; the Model T appeared in 1908, and Ford’s landholdings grew as his automobile business transformed American transportation. Archived records note that by 1909, Ford owned more than 2,000 acres in the general Dearborn area. The Fair Lane grounds themselves were originally conventional Midwestern farmland, with small cleared plots and virgin forest through which the Rouge River meandered. Ford and his wife also treated the landscape as a natural bird and game sanctuary, thus preserving most of its rural character.Historical accounts suggest that Ford bought large tracts of land in Dearborn Township in 1909 and, during the summer, visited architect Frank Lloyd Wright in Oak Park, Illinois.The visit resulted in a commission for a large estate along the Rouge River, though the architectural project progressed slowly and ultimately changed hands.In 1913, Preliminary architectural work began, but Fords reportedly became dissatisfied with the initial plans. Following this, William H. Van Tine of Pittsburgh later became the architect, and the construction of the mansion began in February 1914. The NPS reported that the construction was completed in the following year and that the Fords first moved into the house in 1916.The federal records describe the completed house as a 200-foot-long mansion with 31,770 square feet of floor space. The exterior was a blend of an early English design and modified Scottish Baronial elements. The interiors, meanwhile, contained 56 rooms, which included a library capable of holding more than 4,000 books and a music room with an elaborate marble and walnut fireplace.During the Fords’ era, the area comprising the home and gardens covered about 1,260 acres. Around 1,180 acres consisted of woodlands, farms and orchards, while gardens, landscaping and lawns occupied the remaining portions. The Rouge River was central to Fair Lane’s design and was crucial to one of Ford’s technological projects there.While his interest in generating his own electric power dated back to about 1909, the permanent concrete dam and small brick powerhouse were ultimately constructed between 1914 and 1915 in tandem with the nearby mansion. According to the NPS , the dam included a fish ladder, thus reflecting the combination of technological experimentation and attention to the property’s wildlife. The dam became a part of that design when landscape designer Jens Jensen later developed Fair Lane’s gardens.Hired by Ford in 1914, Jensen helped connect the formal regions surrounding the mansion with the existing landscape. He developed gardens of the estate and a master plan that incorporated the river, woodland and other rural features. Historical records consider Fair Lane an important example of Jensen’s landscape design, with the grounds becoming an integral part of the property’s historic character rather than functioning merely as a decoration around the house.The estate also had an infrastructure that allowed it to operate with a degree of independence. The power plant was connected to the house by a tunnel approximately 300 feet long, while the wider property included support buildings and facilities associated with the household and surrounding land. These features, alongside the farms, orchards and gardens, made Fair Lane an estate that blended domestic life, agriculture, landscape design and technology.Fair Lane remained the principal home of Henry and Clara Ford for the rest of their lives. On 7 April 1947, Henry Ford died at the estate, while Clara continued to live there until her death in 1950.Six years after Clara Ford’s death, the Ford Motor Company presented the house and 210 acres of the estate to the University of Michigan for development of its Dearborn campus. Records suggest that the university used the house as a conference centre. The federal archived records date the property’s recognition to 1966, when Fair Lane was designated a National Historic Landmark. The designation recognised not just the house but also the property’s national significance through its association with Ford, as well as its architectural and landscape qualities.In the later years, Fair Lane became closely associated with the University of Michigan-Dearborn, and the surviving estate reflected only part of the enormous landholding Ford accumulated around Dearborn. The designated National Historic Landmark district encompassed about 356 acres, which was considerably smaller than either Ford’s broader 2,000-plus-acre holdings or the approximately 1,260-acre Fair Lane property described for Ford’s period. This delta simply reflects decades of municipal expansion and university campus growth, which subdivided outer agricultural plots. The surviving landscape, however, still preserved the central elements that defined the estate: the mansion overlooking the Rouge River, the designed grounds, and the dam.
Article Summary: Henry Ford bought more than 2,000 acres of land around Dearborn, Michigan in the early 20th century. Eventually, the land turned into the setting for Fair Lane, the home he shared with his wife, Clara. In 1966, 19 yearsafter Ford’s death, Fair Lane was recognised as a National Historic Landmark.

Article Title: Oscar-winning actor Paul Newman gave 7.5 Connecticut acres to Westport in 1997; after his death, it helped form a 38-acre preserve with land bought for $3.75 million
Article Text:
Oscar-winning actor Paul Newman gave 7.5 Connecticut acres to Westport in 1997. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A gift rooted in Newman's own life

Where woodland meets river

Paul Newman donated 7.5 acres to the town, while another 29.9 acres were acquired from the Poses family for $3.75 million. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A memorial that became public land

Hollywood stars have often left behind buildings, awards and film memorabilia, but Paul Newman left something quieter: a piece of woodland in his adopted hometown of Westport, Connecticut. In 1997, the Oscar-winning actor donated 7.5 acres beside his home to the town, helping protect a larger area of open space that later became the Newman/Poses Nature Preserve.
