Following Newman’s death in 2008, his family supported naming the preserve in his honour, transforming land once connected to his private life into a public natural retreat.According to the Connecticut Post, the Newman/Poses Nature Preserve is a roughly 38-acre tract at the corner of Bayberry Lane, Coleytown Road and Easton Road in Westport. In 1997, Paul Newman donated 7.5 acres to the town, while another 29.9 acres were acquired from the Poses family for $3.75 million. The property includes woods, a meadow, wetlands and the Aspetuck River, and is maintained as open space by the Aspetuck Land Trust.Newman's connection to the property was personal. He and his wife, actress Joanne Woodward, had made Westport their home, and their children grew up exploring the land around the family property.Lissy Newman later recalled walking through the woods with her father and talking with him there. For the Newman family, preserving the land was less about creating a memorial than about protecting a place full of memories.The actor had also developed a reputation for supporting conservation in his community and was a longtime supporter of the Aspetuck Land Trust, which would eventually help maintain the preserve. After Newman’s death in September 2008, his daughters Lissy and Clea worked with the land trust and town officials to turn the already protected property into a formally designated nature preserve. Although Newman had generally been reluctant to have public places named after him, his family made an exception for the woodland because of his personal connection to the land and his enjoyment of walking there. In 2010, Westport’s Representative Town Meeting unanimously approved the name Newman/Poses Nature Preserve, honouring both Newman and the Poses family, whose land had also become part of the preserve.The preserve is more than a patch of trees. Its ecological value comes partly from the mixture of habitats packed into a relatively small area. The site includes woodland, meadow, wetlands, streams and the Aspetuck River. Trails wind through these different environments, while some wetland crossings use raised boardwalks to reduce disturbance. The town has kept the area for passive recreation, allowing activities such as walking and, in permitted areas, fishing, while prohibiting development.The preserve's mix of woodland and open habitat supports a range of wildlife. Contemporary reporting on the site described birds, chipmunks, squirrels and coyotes, while state wildlife officials noted that its combination of native grasses, wetlands, streams and meadow provided habitat useful for feeding, nesting and seasonal activity. The area also supports turtles, including the North American wood turtle and eastern box turtle, which can use open-canopy upland areas for summer foraging.Research published in Ecosphere has more recently reinforced the importance of protecting Connecticut's forest habitat. Examining bird communities across the state, researchers found that increasing forest fragmentation was associated with declines in community density, while habitat characteristics influenced species richness. The findings underline how retaining sizeable, functioning habitat can be important for birds living in an increasingly developed landscape.In 2011, the Newman/Poses Nature Preserve was accessible to the public. Visitors were taken on a tour of the trails that passed through woods and meadow and even along the Aspetuck River. The property was owned by the town and managed by the Aspetuck Land Trust, turning land once used mainly by neighbours into a public space. Newman's life history makes the narrative especially relevant. Newman was known for Hollywood glamour, but he also spent his later years on philanthropy and auto racing, and remained deeply devoted to the places he called home.What began in 1997 as a 7.5-acre donation eventually became part of a much larger protected area. The $3.75-million purchase of the neighbouring Poses property expanded the preserve, while Newman’s death in 2008 brought renewed attention to his connection with the land. In 2010, the community named the protected area the Newman/Poses Nature Preserve. Today, the preserve encompasses nearly 38 acres of woodland, meadow and river habitat, preserving a piece of Newman’s legacy for both people and wildlife.
Article Summary: Oscar-winning actor donated 7.5 acres to the town of Westport, Connecticut, in 1997. Another 29.9 acres were acquired from the Poses family for $3.75 million. Newman/Poses Nature Preserve is a roughly 38-acre tract at the corner of Bayberry Lane, Coleytown Road and Easton Road.

Article Title: 'Trump furious about leaks': US orders polygraph test for top officials, reports
Article Text:
50 US Joint Staff officials face polygraph tests

US government investigators subjected roughly 50 members of the Joint Staff to polygraph tests over leaks to journalists. The investigation centred on leaks about dwindling US stocks of advanced weapons, according to reports.According to multiple media reports, members of the Joint Staff were tested in August after media reports detailed shortages of crucial munitions, including long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors, the Times reported, citing officials briefed on the move.The tests sought to determine whether military officers and civilian employees had disclosed classified information to journalists, including details about diminished US munitions stocks.CBS News reported that several dozen people had also been tested earlier in the summer, including officials at US Central Command and other combatant commands.Polygraphs are routinely used every few years to recertify security clearances for officials with access to top-secret information or special access programmes. However, officials told CBS News that the number of people tested in this case was highly unusual.The New York Times reported that the US Joint Staff has between 1,500 and 2,000 officers and officials, coordinating operations, policy and war plans with combatant commanders around the world.Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell, meanwhile, said the department “does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters but takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly.”The questions reportedly covered a range of national security matters. Sources quoted by CBS News said that no one failed the questions specifically aimed at determining whether they had leaked information to the media.President Donald Trump was furious about the leaks, according to three CBS News sources who spoke on condition of anonymity. One source said only a very small group of people had access to the classified weapons information, raising concerns over whether anyone could be acting as a foreign intelligence asset.Not all senior officials were tested. A senior Pentagon official told CBS News that chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine was not subjected to a polygraph.The scope of the testing comes after defence secretary Pete Hegseth announced in July that the Pentagon and Justice Department had formed a joint task force to identify and prosecute suspected leakers. “When a leak of department information occurs today, it's critical that we provide the Department of Justice and other partners in federal law enforcement — including the FBI — with actionable information as quickly as possible,” Hegseth said. “Leaked information risks lives.”The FBI was not involved in the latest round of polygraph tests, with the US military conducting the investigation itself.Federal law and Pentagon regulations place restrictions on the use of polygraphs and require procedural safeguards, including consent in certain investigative circumstances
Article Summary: US government investigators subjected roughly 50 members of the Joint Staff to polygraph tests over leaks to journalists. The investigation centred on leaks about dwindling US stocks of advanced weapons, according to reports.Polygraphs are routinely used every few years to recertify security clearances for officials.

Article Title: Trump eyes Pentagon leadership changes as frustration over Iran war grows: Report
Article Text:
The Pentagon, headquarters of the US department of war (Photo: AP).

At least four candidates have reportedly emerged as potential replacements for former US army secretary Dan Driscoll, as the Trump administration moves to fill the post following his resignation.Among those being considered is Marc Andersen, assistant secretary of the army for financial management and comptroller, whom President Donald Trump has already been briefed on, NBC News reported, citing sources.Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson and a former Army officer, is also reportedly expected to receive the backing of defence secretary Pete Hegseth.Another option under discussion is for someone else to become Army secretary while Parnell takes on a senior role in running the branch, NBC reported.This comes as Driscoll resigned last week following repeated clashes with Hegseth over several issues linked to the Iran war and formally left the administration after serving for 18 months. Trump on Thursday announced that Adam Telle, the army’s assistant secretary for civil works, would serve as acting secretary.However, it remains unclear how quickly a permanent replacement will be nominated.The search comes as the army faces a broader leadership vacuum.Its chief of staff, gen. Randy George, was asked to step down by Hegseth earlier this year, while the branch is also under pressure amid more than six months of war with Iran.Separately, according to sources cited by news agency Reuters, the White House has been reviewing possible candidates to replace the deputy secretary of war, Steve Feinberg.The review reportedly began as early as June and included discussions with senior senators about whether potential nominees would have enough support for confirmation. Reuters said the review was still ongoing as of late August.However, the sources said no decision had been made to remove Feinberg and did not provide a reason for the review or identify potential replacements.White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly dismissed the reports, saying: "These so-called anonymous 'sources' have no idea what they are talking about."The Pentagon also denied that a replacement process was underway. Hegseth said Feinberg has his full support and “isn’t going anywhere.”The possibility of further changes comes amid growing frustration within the administration over the Iran war.Trump has increasingly expressed frustration over the lack of progress in the six-month-old conflict, which has developed into a costly standoff between the US and Iran.
Article Summary: Dan Driscoll resigned last week following clashes with defence secretary Pete Hegseth over several issues linked to the Iran war. Among those being considered is Marc Andersen, assistant secretary of the army for financial management and comptroller. Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson and a former Army officer, also reportedly expected to receive the backing of defence secretary.

Article Title: US man duct-taped to seat after attacking passenger mid-flight, hurling racial abuse
Article Text:
A photo shared by one of the passengers, Richard Olenick, showed the man had multiple loops of tape around his wrists, torso and head

An allegedly disruptive passenger was duct-taped to a passenger seat on an American Airlines flight from Dallas-Fort Worth to Newark that made an unexpected stop in Baltimore late Thursday.A photo shared by one of the passengers showed the man had multiple loops of tape around his wrists, torso and head.About two hours into the flight, witnesses told CBS News how the situation suddenly escalated, with the passenger allegedly yelling and attacking the man seated next to him by grabbing his neck.Two passengers, including retired law enforcement officer Juan Mejia, intervened to restrain him. With the help of a flight attendant, they used zip ties and duct tape to secure the passenger to his seat.Witnesses also alleged that the passenger hurled a racial slur and homophobic remarks at a flight attendant when she attempted to calm the situation. He later became violent, prompting the crew to restrain him and divert the flight to Baltimore.In Baltimore, he was reportedly removed by law enforcement, after which the flight continued to Newark.
Article Summary: A photo shared by one of the passengers, Richard Olenick, showed the man had multiple loops of tape around his wrists, torso and head. About two hours into the flight, witnesses told CBS News how the situation suddenly escalated, with the passenger allegedly yelling and attacking the man seated next to him by grabbing his neck. With the help of a flight attendant, they used zip ties and duct tape to secure the passenger to his seat.

Article Title: New York City shooting: Man fatally shot on Brooklyn Bridge after 'ignoring orders to drop weapon'
Article Text:
Brooklyn Bridge P​olice Shooting

Also Read |

A knife-wielding man walking on the cables of New York City’s iconic Brooklyn Bridge was fatally shot after he allegedly ignored police orders to drop the weapon, authorities said on Friday (local time).The man, whose name has not yet been released, was shot after moving within feet of an officer who was trying to help him climb down.According to Gerard Dowling, commanding officer of the New York City Police Department’s Emergency Services Unit, the man told the police rescue team to kill him and claimed he had a bomb.“The officers spoke to him for about an hour... they wanted to help him and bring him down and told him to drop the knife multiple times. The officers began to move backwards away from the male when he began to climb down, but were not able to move as quickly as the subject, who was approaching them,” Dowling told a news conference later.He added that the man came within three feet of an officer and raised his arm, with the knife extended toward the officer. At that point, another officer shot him once. The rescue team then brought the man down, and he later died at a hospital.Police body cameras recorded the encounter. In addition to the knife, a flashlight was recovered.When a reporter asked whether police had found a bomb, Dowling replied that was part of the ongoing investigation.New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani posted online that officers responded after receiving a 911 call about a man “who appeared to be attempting to jump from the bridge.”“As is standard when an NYPD officer discharges a firearm, the department will conduct an internal investigation, and body-worn camera footage will be released,” Mamdani said.The Brooklyn Bridge, which opened in 1883, is a cable-supported suspension bridge connecting Manhattan and Brooklyn.Its towers rise 276.5 feet (84 metres) above the water. It was not immediately clear how high above the water the man and the police officers were when the incident occurred.
Article Summary: A knife-wielding man walking on the cables of New York City’s iconic Brooklyn Bridge was fatally shot after he allegedly ignored police orders to drop the weapon. The man, whose name has not yet been released, was shot after moving within feet of an officer who was trying to help him climb down. He told the police rescue team to kill him and claimed he had a bomb.

Article Title: Pizza, meth & guns: Indian national illegally living in US charged with drug trafficking
Article Text:
Indian national charged over drug trafficking, illegal arms from pizza outlet in US. Photo credit: IANS, DOJ

An Indian national unlawfully living in the United States has been charged with allegedly distributing methamphetamine from a pizza outlet in California, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) said.He has also been charged with possessing firearms in connection with drug trafficking.According to court documents, 50-year-old Kawal Preet Singh sold wholesale quantities of methamphetamine from a Round Table Pizza restaurant he operated in Dinuba, California, while armed with illegal firearms.A federal grand jury returned an indictment against Singh, charging him with “distribution of methamphetamine, possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, and possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime”, US attorney Eric Grant announced, according to the DOJ.The charges follow a federal investigation into organised Indian crime in California’s Central Valley, which identified Singh as a subject, the DOJ said.On August 18, federal agents searched Singh’s home and business and seized more than 40 pounds of methamphetamine, three firearms and more than $10,000 in cash, according to the department.The DOJ said Singh faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years and a maximum of life in prison, along with a fine of up to $10 million, if convicted on the drug-trafficking charges.He also faces a mandatory minimum of five years in prison, to be served consecutively to any other sentence, and up to life imprisonment for possessing a firearm in furtherance of drug trafficking.The department stressed that “The charges are only allegations; the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.”The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Homeland Security Investigations conducted the investigation.The case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force initiative, described by the DOJ as a “whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organisations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad.”
Article Summary: Kawal Preet Singh, 50, allegedly sold methamphetamine from a pizza outlet in California. He has also been charged with possessing firearms in connection with drug trafficking. The charges follow a federal investigation into organised Indian crime in California’s Central Valley.

Article Title: 'Small potatoes for us': Trump plays down Iran conflict, issues fresh warning
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump

US President Donald Trump on Friday issued a fresh threat to Iran, saying that the America could "hit" its heavily fortified underground nuclear site "very soon."Speaking to reporters at the Oval Office, Trump warned that Pickaxe Mountain could be targeted if the US detects activity there."We may hit Pickaxe very soon because if there was anything going on with Pickaxe," Trump said, adding that US intelligence was closely monitoring activity at the site."We know everybody that's moving at Pickaxe; we know everybody that's moving everywhere all over Iran. And if anything goes bad, we hit them; we hit them hard," Trump said.He also defended Unites States' military campaign in Iran and said that its primary objective was to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapon."We're in five months now. And you know what we did in five months? They're not going to have a nuclear weapon; that's what we did," Trump said."Iran will not have a nuclear weapon because if they did, you probably wouldn't be standing here very long," he added.Pickaxe Mountain is located near Iran’s heavily damaged Natanz uranium-enrichment facility and is described as a heavily fortified underground complex comprising two deeply buried tunnel systems.The Wall Street Journal had earlier reported that Israeli intelligence believes Iran has moved thousands of centrifuges to the deeply buried site.The facility’s underground construction is believed to make it significantly more resistant to conventional aerial strikes. Any potential US decision to target the site could therefore mark a major escalation in the campaign against Iran’s nuclear infrastructure.Asked about his deputy JD Vance's assertion that months of on-and-off attacks in the Middle East are not a war, Trump said that conflict in Iran is “small potatoes”“I can understand what he’s saying,” Trump said.“I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us. It's not a big thing," he added.His remarks came days after US Central Command said American forces had completed a fresh wave of strikes against Iranian military targets.According to CENTCOM, the operations targeted facilities linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, including air-defence installations, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites.CENTCOM said the strikes followed what it described as recent “attempted attacks” by the IRGC on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and US service members.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump on Friday issued a fresh threat to Iran, saying that the America could "hit" its heavily fortified underground nuclear site "very soon" He also defended Unites States' military campaign in Iran and said that its primary objective was to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapon.

Article Title: In 2011, a 39,000-sq-ft Michigan school on a former Air Force base sold for $40,000; 15 years later, one wing has become 5 homes and the 19-acre property is asking $450,000
Article Text:
A former Michigan school sold for $40,000 in 2011 is now listed for $450,000. (Photo: Realtor.com)

From $40,000 sale to $450,000 asking price

One wing of the 39,000-square-foot former school has been transformed into five homes. (Photo: Realtor.com)

One wing has become five homes

The former K.I. Sawyer Air Force Base school sits on nearly 20 acres of Michigan land. (Photo: Realtor.com)

The gym and classrooms are still intact

The unusual property still features its original gymnasium and multiple former classrooms. (Photo: Realtor.com)

36 garage spaces add to the appeal

A $40,000 school purchase has evolved into a $450,000 redevelopment opportunity 15 years later. (Photo: Realtor.com)

A property waiting for its next chapter

A former school building on a Michigan Air Force base has undergone a remarkable transformation since it was sold for just $40,000 in 2011. Fifteen years later, the 39,000-square-foot property has one wing converted into five residential units and is now listed for $450,000.The unusual property at 530 Mitchell St. in Gwinn, Michigan, is offering potential buyers an opportunity to turn a former educational facility into a residential, commercial or community-focused project.Situated on 19.38 acres at the former K.I. Sawyer Air Force Base, the one-story building dates back to 1960 and still retains much of its original school layout, including classrooms and a gymnasium.According to Realtor, property records show the building last changed hands in 2011, when it sold for only $40,000. At the time, however, the sprawling structure remained largely in its original condition.The property has since undergone significant work, with one of its three wings converted into multiple residences. It is now being marketed for $450,000, giving it an asking price of roughly $12 per square foot based on the building's approximately 39,000-square-foot gross area.The listing, held by Dylan Willey of Coldwell Banker Schmidt Realtors, describes the property as a potentially valuable opportunity for a “visionary buyer or investor.”The building is divided into three wings, with Wing A receiving the most extensive renovation.That section has been converted into five separate living spaces, accompanied by an attached garage. The largest residence features two bedrooms and two bathrooms, including an en suite bathroom.Photos show an updated kitchen with wooden cabinetry, dark countertops and a large central island. The kitchen connects to the living area, creating an open-plan residential space that contrasts sharply with the property's institutional origins.Wing A also includes two additional two-bedroom residences, one with in-unit laundry, along with an open-concept studio and a four-bedroom, 1.5-bathroom residence.Altogether, the converted section contributes to the property's current configuration of 12 bedrooms and 8.5 bathrooms.While one portion has been transformed into housing, much of the former school remains unfinished.Wing B offers a glimpse into the building's past, retaining its original gymnasium, four former classrooms and a studio space. A separate guest area includes two bedrooms, a bunk room and a bathroom.For a buyer willing to take on another ambitious renovation, these spaces could potentially be converted into additional housing or adapted for an entirely different purpose.Wing C remains largely in its original condition and includes storage areas, group meeting spaces and a large garage.The property's enormous footprint extends to its parking capacity. The listing records 36 garage spaces, in addition to covered parking and direct garage access.The property is also connected to electricity and natural gas and has public water and sanitary sewer services, giving a future owner access to key infrastructure.The nearly 20-acre parcel provides considerable outdoor space around the former school, adding another potential dimension to the redevelopment opportunity.Despite the work already completed, the property remains very much a work in progress. Its combination of converted residences and untouched institutional spaces leaves room for a buyer to determine what comes next.The listing suggests several possibilities, including expanding the residential component, developing community storage or pursuing another “creative” vision.For a buyer willing to embrace its unusual history, the former K.I. Sawyer Air Force Base school offers something few conventional properties can: nearly 39,000 square feet of building space, almost 20 acres of land and a partially completed conversion into homes.What began as a $40,000 acquisition in 2011 has evolved into a $450,000 redevelopment opportunity, with much of the building's next chapter still waiting to be written.
Article Summary: The one-story building dates back to 1960 and still retains much of its original school layout, including classrooms and a gymnasium. The building is divided into three wings, with Wing A receiving the most extensive renovation. That section has been converted into five separate living spaces, accompanied by an attached garage.

Article Title: ‘Growing differences between military, Asif Zardari’: Self-exiled Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain makes big claim
Article Text:
Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain (File photo)

Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain has alleged a "silent struggle" is underway between Pakistan's powerful military establishment and President Asif Ali Zardari , warning that a debate over creating new provinces could push the country into a major political and security crisis.The founder of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) claimed that discussions were underway on a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment, which could include provisions for the creation of new provinces.“Discussions on the creation of new provinces have been raised by interior minister Mohsin Naqvi and DG-ISPR. The proposed constitutional changes reflect growing differences between President Asif Ali Zardari and the military leadership. A political deadlock could lead to serious constitutional consequences, including the imposition of martial law or the formation of an interim government,” Hussain said in a TikTok message on September 2.Referring to the earlier 26th and 27th Amendments, he alleged that political parties had previously reached agreements to facilitate their passage.Hussain also questioned the prolonged foreign stay of Zardari, the husband of slain former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto and father of ex-foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari."The President had travelled to Austria in connection for his son Bilawal Zardari’s wedding and is currently in London. There was also an hour-long meeting between Zardari and Naqvi in London, claiming that an important message was conveyed to the President," he added.Hussain further cautioned that tensions between the Pakistan military and Sindhi nationalist groups could escalate into widespread unrest. Referring to the situation in Balochistan, Hussain said violence between security forces and Baloch fighters was continuing and called for greater political consideration for the Baloch people.He warned that if Pakistan descended into a broader civil conflict, foreign powers, including the US and UK, would not come to its rescue, and urged Pakistanis to heed his warnings.
Article Summary: Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain has alleged a "silent struggle" is underway between Pakistan's powerful military establishment and President Asif Ali Zardari. The founder of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) claimed that discussions were underway on a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment.

Article Title: 25 Pakistani military personnel killed in Balochistan attacks, BLA claims
Article Text:
Balochistan: BLA claims 25 Pakistani military personnel killed in two attacks (Picture from X)

The Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) on Thursday claimed responsibility for two attacks in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, saying 25 Pakistani military personnel were killed and three military vehicles destroyed.According to The Balochistan Post, the BLA spokesperson said fighters targeted a military convoy at Ziarat Cross, attacking vehicles and destroying two of them, including a military truck.The militant group initially claimed that 18 personnel were killed in the attack, with the death toll later rising to 25.The BLA also released a one-minute-and-11-second video trailer through Hakkal, its official media channel, which it said showed footage from the Ziarat Cross attack.The footage purportedly shows armed fighters near burning Pakistani military vehicles, with bodies visible at the site and weapons being seized. The BLA said it would release the complete video later.In a separate operation in the Hajika area of Surab, the group’s Special Tactical Operations Squad (STOS) remotely detonated an explosives-laden vehicle, destroying a military vehicle and killing seven personnel, according to the BLA statement.
Article Summary: Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) claims responsibility for two attacks in Pakistan's Balochistan province. BLA says 25 Pakistani military personnel were killed and three military vehicles destroyed. The militant group also released a one-minute-and-11-second video trailer through Hakkal.

Article Title: ‘6ft by 8ft cell, brown drinking water’: What Imran Khan’s jail cell is like
Article Text:
The report said visitors have been barred and Khan has been confined to his cell for as much as 23 hours a day.

Former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan is being held in what has been described as harsh conditions at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail, with reports alleging prolonged isolation, limited access to reading material and restrictions on contact with his family.According to a report by The Times UK, Khan is being kept in a 6ft by 8ft cell typically used for prisoners on death row. The report said the 73-year-old has no reading material apart from the Quran and is being provided “soiled brown water” to drink.His sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, have reportedly been unable to meet their father in person since 2022 and have at times been prevented from speaking to him by telephone for months. They have described his living conditions as inhumane “torture tactics”.The report said visitors have been barred and Khan has been confined to his cell for as much as 23 hours a day.The reported restrictions have also become the subject of repeated legal challenges by Khan’s family.His sister Uzma Khan filed a fresh contempt petition in the Supreme Court on Wednesday, alleging that authorities have failed to comply with an August 18 order concerning Khan’s access to his family.According to The Express Tribune, the petition names Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Adiala Jail Superintendent Sajid Baig, Punjab Inspector General of Prisons Mian Salik Jalal and other senior officials as respondents.The August 18 order had directed authorities to facilitate virtual communication between Khan and his sons and allow his sisters to meet him weekly. However, Uzma said she was denied a scheduled visit on Tuesday, while telephone communication between Khan and his sons has remained restricted since March.The petition also alleges that authorities failed to establish the infrastructure required for bi-weekly telephone calls with Sulaiman and Kasim.The latest dispute follows an earlier contempt petition over the alleged non-compliance with the Supreme Court’s direction to transfer Khan to Shifa International Hospital for medical evaluation. He was instead taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on August 21 before being returned to Adiala Jail after doctors declared him “medically fit”. Authorities have cited security concerns for the decision.
Article Summary: Imran Khan is being held in what has been described as harsh conditions at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail. Reports allege prolonged isolation, limited access to reading material and restrictions on contact with his family. His sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, have reportedly been unable to meet their father in person since 2022.

Article Title: Pakistan: Imran Khan's sister files fresh contempt plea over denied jail visits
Article Text: Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan's sister Uzma Khan on Wednesday filed a fresh contempt of court petition in the Supreme Court, alleging non-enforcement of previous judicial directives issued by the country's apex court.In her petition, Uzma named several high-ranking officials, including Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and Adiala (Rawalpindi Central Jail) Superintendent Sajid Baig, as respondents.According to the Express Tribune, the petition was filed after the Supreme Court's August 18 instructions, which mandated virtual communication between Imran Khan and his sons, alongside weekly access for his sisters, failed to materialise.The plea said that Uzma Khan was denied a scheduled visit on Tuesday and noted that audio communication with his sons has remained restricted since March.The petition alleged that authorities neglected to establish the necessary infrastructure enabling bi-weekly telephone calls with his sons, Kasim Khan and Sulaiman Khan, as previously ordered by the bench.Earlier, Uzma had filed another contempt application addressing government non-compliance regarding a separate instruction within the August 18 order, which directed that Imran Khan be moved to Shifa International Hospital for medical care.Under the original August 18 decision, the Supreme Court instructed that the former premier be transferred to Shifa International Hospital for clinical evaluation by a multidisciplinary medical panel while simultaneously granting visitation rights.Following the orders, authorities transferred Imran Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on August 21. He was, however, sent back to Adiala Jail shortly after medical personnel declared him to be "medically fit".Reacting to the developments, the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) lambasted prison administrators for barring relatives from seeing the party founder, characterising the restrictions as a flagrant breach of mandates issued by both the Supreme Court and the Islamabad High Court, as reported by another Pakistan-based daily, Dawn.
Article Summary: Imran Khan's sister Uzma Khan has filed a contempt of court petition in the Supreme Court. She alleges non-enforcement of previous judicial directives issued by the country's apex court. Uzma named several high-ranking officials, including Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and Adiala (Rawalpindi Central Jail) Superintendent Sajid Baig as respondents.

Article Title: Pak pleads for dialogue after India stands firm on suspending Indus Water Treaty
Article Text:
Indus Waters treaty representational image

India rejects tribunal ruling

Water, terrorism and the SCO

NEW DELHI: Just days after India rejected an international tribunal's ruling on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) and dismissed its jurisdiction, Pakistan on Wednesday urged New Delhi to engage "constructively" within the framework of the 1960 water-sharing agreement.According to news agency PTI, Pakistan foreign office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said the Permanent Court of Arbitration had reaffirmed that the treaty remained fully enforced and binding. Pakistan, he said, would take “all possible measures” to ensure the decision was implemented.Andrabi said Pakistan remained committed to implementing the treaty in letter and spirit in accordance with its language and provisions.Pakistan will continue to urge India to reciprocate with the same approach whereby the treaty is upheld in letter and spirit and in its full legal documented provisions, he said, according to PTI.Pakistan had approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in March 2026, seeking a determination on the status of the treaty after India placed it in abeyance.India, however, has consistently rejected the jurisdiction of the arbitration process.On Monday, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) said, “India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body.”“India's decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance remains in force,” the ministry said.MEA said the Court of Arbitration had issued what it termed an award on May 15, 2026, concerning maximum pondage supplemental to an earlier award on issues of general interpretation of the IWT."This so-called Court was constituted by the World Bank in patent breach of the terms of the Treaty and India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body", the ministry stated.India has maintained that the establishment of the arbitral body itself violates the IWT and that it has no jurisdiction over India’s sovereign decision to place the treaty in abeyance.The dispute also featured indirectly at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit, in Bishkek, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for action against countries that use terrorism as an instrument of state policy.“We cannot remain confined to an action-reaction approach,” Modi said, calling for the dismantling of terrorist ecosystems, including funding networks, recruitment pipelines and territorial sanctuaries.Pakistan prime minister Shehbaz Sharif, speaking at the summit, described water as the region’s “lifeblood” and said it “must never be weaponised”.“The treaties governing our shared waters are solemn, binding international commitments. They are not matters of political convenience to be cast aside at your will. They must be honoured unconditionally, in both letter and spirit,” Sharif said, according to Dawn.India placed the IWT in abeyance following the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 people were killed. The Cabinet Committee on Security took the decision on April 23, 2025, with New Delhi saying the conditions underlying the treaty had fundamentally changed.India has said the treaty will remain in abeyance until Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably abjures its support for cross-border terrorism”.
Article Summary: Pakistan urges New Delhi to engage "constructively" within the framework of the 1960 water-sharing agreement. Pakistan had approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in March 2026, seeking a determination on the status of the treaty. India, however, has consistently rejected the jurisdiction of the arbitration process.

Article Title: Leadership gaps cloud Pakistan's human rights oversight system
Article Text:
Pakistan human rights faces pending vacancy

NCHR’s legal status under question

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is most important for an effective human rights body? Strong leadership Independence Transparency Accountability 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan’s human rights oversight framework is facing growing uncertainty as key commissions continue to function without permanent leadership or full membership, raising concerns over their independence and effectiveness.The previous National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) completed its four-year term in November 2025, but a new commission has yet to be fully constituted, news agency ANI cited in its report. The National Commission on the Status of Women (NCSW) is also functioning under an acting chairperson.Former NCHR chairperson Khawar Mumtaz criticised and warned that prolonged reliance on temporary arrangements could weaken the autonomy and performance of independent rights bodies.Human rights activist Peter Jacob said Parliament passed legislation establishing the National Commission for Minorities Rights in December 2025, but appointments to the body remain incomplete.The National Commission on the Rights of the Child has also faced vacancies. The Ministry of Human Rights invited applications in July 2026 for members representing Punjab, Islamabad and Balochistan, The Express Tribune reported.An amendment to the National Commission for Human Rights Act in 2026 introduced Section 4A, allowing a chairperson to continue for up to 120 days after the expiry of their term or until a successor is appointed.NCHR Chairperson Rabiya Javeri Agha maintained that the commission remains operationally effective, pointing to additional staff recruited two years ago. She said the extension of the chairperson’s tenure was made under the law and reflected practices followed by human rights institutions internationally. Questions regarding the constitution of a new commission, she said, should be directed to the government, according to The Express Tribune.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s human rights oversight framework is facing growing uncertainty. Key commissions continue to function without permanent leadership or full membership. The previous National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) completed its four-year term in November 2025. A new commission has yet to be fully constituted, news agency ANI cited in its report.

Article Title: Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi get slight relief as Pak HC bars solitary confinement
Article Text:
Pak HC intervenes over Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi's detention, bars solitary confinement

A Pakistan high court on Tuesday directed authorities at Rawalpindi Jail to ensure that former prime minister Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi are not held in solitary confinement. The ruling also set out provisions for Khan's family meetings, phone calls, reading material and medical care.The Islamabad High Court (IHC), while hearing petitions challenging the couple's alleged solitary confinement, directed the jail authorities to allow Khan's family members to meet him in line with prison rules and arrange telephone conversations with his sons.Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro also ordered the jail to provide Khan with newspapers and books every day and ensure access to medical facilities as prescribed under jail rules. Rawalpindi's Aiala jail superintendent has been asked to implement the directions and submit a compliance report within 15 days, according to the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The court had earlier reserved its verdict on August 6 on separate petitions filed by Khan's sister Aleema Khanum and Bushra Bibi's daughter Mubashra Khawar Maneka. The IHC also held the petitions challenging the alleged solitary confinement to be maintainable.The 73-year-old cricketer-turned-politician and his wife have been in custody since August 2023 and is serving prison terms in corruption and related cases. Khan's Tehreek-e-Insaf party and supporters have maintained that the cases are politically motivated, while the government has rejected allegations of mistreatment.Bushra Bibi was first jailed in January 2024 after being convicted in a corruption-related case. She was released on bail in October that year after nearly nine months in custody but was arrested again in January 2025 following another corruption conviction. She remains at Adiala Jail.The IHC order comes as Khan's detention and medical treatment remain the subject of separate proceedings before the Supreme Court.On Monday, the Supreme Court declined an application by Khan's sister Uzma Khan seeking an early hearing of her contempt petition against government officials over the alleged failure to comply with an earlier order concerning his transfer to a private hospital, Dawn reported.Pakistan's Supreme Court had on August 18 ordered that Khan be shifted to the privately run Shifa International Hospital after concerns were raised by his family and supporters over his health, including an eye condition diagnosed earlier this year.Instead, Khan was taken to the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on the night of August 20-21 for a medical procedure and diagnostic examinations and was later returned to Adiala Jail.Uzma Khan's petition contends that this breached the Supreme Court's direction that Khan remain admitted at the Islamabad hospital until the next hearing on September 16. The government has defended the decision, citing security concerns.Two specialists from Shifa International Hospital also participated in Khan's eye examination at PIMS, according to the hospital administration, as reported by Dawn.Uzma Khan had sought an earlier hearing, arguing that further delay could affect the enforcement of the Supreme Court's order. The Supreme Court, however, rejected the request under its case-fixation policy, noting that 94 other criminal original petitions in the same category were pending, Dawn reported.The contempt petition is listed for September 16 before a three-member bench comprising Justices Shahid Waheed, Naeem Akhtar Afghan and Ishtiaq Ibrahim. The bench is also scheduled to hear other matters concerning Khan's health and family meetings.
Article Summary: Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi have been in custody since August 2023. The couple is serving prison terms in corruption and related cases. The Islamabad High Court ordered the jail authorities to allow Khan's family members to meet him in line with prison rules.

Article Title: Pakistan power crisis deepens as Karachi reels from 24-hour blackouts
Article Text:
​Karachi reels under deepening power crisis as blackouts last up to 24 hours

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you agree that electricity should be treated as an essential service? Yes No Unsure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Karachi's electricity crisis has intensified, with residents in several parts of the city reporting outages lasting up to 24 hours. Rights activists in Pakistan have warned that prolonged loadshedding is placing a growing burden on low-income families.According to Dawn, the issue was raised at a press conference at the Karachi Press Club organised by the Civil Society Collective for Clean Energy for Karachi. Speakers said extended power cuts were disrupting basic household activities, education and work, while also worsening access to water and affecting hygiene.Residents of North Karachi, Nazimabad and parts of Gulistan-i-Jauhar reported between 16 and 24 hours of loadshedding, ANI said. Protests and traffic disruptions were also reported in Lyari and other parts of the old city during the week beginning August 24.The speakers cited K-Electric's published outage schedule, saying more than 615 feeders were listed for power cuts of up to 12 hours a day. They claimed this could affect nearly a third of the city's feeders.Qazi Khizer of the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan said the prolonged outages were having a particularly severe impact on working-class communities.He said electricity shortages were also contributing to rising mental stress and argued that reliable electricity "should be treated as an essential service rather than a privilege".Karachi Union of Journalists president Tahir Hassan Khan questioned whether K-Electric's privatisation had delivered the improvements promised to consumers.He said claims of technological and operational progress had not translated into "dependable electricity supplies".
Article Summary: Residents of North Karachi, Nazimabad and parts of Gulistan-i-Jauhar reported between 16 and 24 hours of loadshedding. Protests and traffic disruptions were also reported in Lyari and other parts of the old city during the week beginning August 24.

Article Title: Pakistan court allows Hindu woman to return home after alleged forced conversion, marriage
Article Text:
Woman returns from Pakistan

'Want to return home'

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that the court made the right decision in allowing Reeta to return to her parents? Yes, it was the right decision. No, she should have been placed in shelter. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A court in Pakistan on Tuesday allowed a 21-year-old Hindu woman to return to her parents after she told the magistrate that she wished to go home of her own free will, days after her family alleged that she had been abducted and pressured to convert to Islam and marry a Muslim man, news agency PTI reported.Shirimati Reeta, a resident of Rana Rajput Colony in Khipro tehsil of Sindh’s Sanghar district, went missing from her hometown last week, according to a complaint filed by her brother Ravi Shankar. He alleged that CCTV footage showed unidentified people taking Reeta from the family home along with valuables and mobile phones on August 24.According to the complaint, Reeta was taken to Gujranwala in Punjab, some 80 kms from Lahore, where she was allegedly pressured to convert to Islam and marry Nazeer Hussain, who was already married.Punjab Police later recovered Reeta and produced her before a judicial magistrate on Monday. The investigating officer sought to place her in Darul Aman, a state-run shelter, claiming that she was unwilling to return to her parents.Her lawyers, Asad Jamal and Kheta Ram, opposed the request and told the court that Reeta wanted to return home with her brother, who was present in court, a court official said.The magistrate then asked Reeta to record her statement under oath. “In her statement, Reeta said that she wanted to return to her parents’ home of her own free will,” the official said.The court subsequently allowed Reeta to leave with her brother and made him responsible for her safe custody and transportation back to the family home in Sanghar.
Article Summary: Shirimati Reeta, a 21-year-old Hindu woman, went missing from her hometown last week. Her family alleged that she had been abducted and pressured to convert to Islam and marry a Muslim man. Police later recovered Reeta and produced her before a judicial magistrate on Monday. The investigating officer sought to place her in Darul Aman, a state-run shelter.

Article Title: Watch: 'Driverless' car crashes into police van after internet outage in Islamabad
Article Text:
In a social media post on Monday, Aalijah sought to clarify that his video was not intended to ridicule Zafar or undermine his work and warned that the technology was not yet ready to be considered completely reliable.

A remotely operated driverless car crashed into a police van in Islamabad after losing its internet connection during a demonstration, with footage of the incident going viral and sparking a wave of memes online.According to local media, the incident took place at D-Chowk, a high-security area in the Pakistani capital, where journalist Muhammad Aalijah was recording a video of a technology-based automated-driving system developed by Abbottabad-based technology enthusiast Ehsan Zafar. The car was being controlled remotely over the internet when a sudden connectivity failure caused its steering to malfunction.Footage shared by Aalijah shows him sitting in the front passenger seat as he explains the vehicle's features while it moves along the road. The remotely controlled steering wheel then appears to lose control, sending the car towards a police van parked nearby.Aalijah can be seen attempting to stop the vehicle by pulling the handbrake, but the car continues moving and bumps into the police vehicle.Aalijah later told Dawn that he had been asked by Zafar to report on his technology-based automated-driving innovation. He attributed the crash to a "technical fault" triggered by an internet disruption.“Everything was fine until a technical fault occurred due to an internet disruption, causing the car to go out of control and crash into a police vehicle,” he said.According to Aalijah, the vehicle was operated remotely through internet and satellite connections. The loss of the internet connection during the demonstration caused the car to become uncontrollable.In a social media post on Monday, Aalijah sought to clarify that his video was not intended to ridicule Zafar or undermine his work.“The sole purpose was to raise awareness and urge people to remain cautious until any new experiment or technology has been thoroughly tested, proven safe and established as a complete success,” he said.“This was a message of caution, not an attempt to discredit anyone.”Aalijah also warned that the technology was not yet ready to be considered completely reliable.“The vehicle was being operated through satellite and internet connections, but during external control, it went out of control as soon as the internet connection was disconnected and collided with a police vehicle,” he wrote.He said the relatively low traffic at D-Chowk limited the potential consequences of the malfunction, but warned that a similar failure on a busy road could have been far more serious.“If the same situation had occurred on a busy road, the consequences could have been extremely dangerous, even fatal,” he said.“This video is not criticism; it is a responsible effort to raise awareness and issue a warning by all means, experiment, but ensure safety first,” he added.
Article Summary: A remotely operated driverless car crashed into a police van in Islamabad after losing its internet connection during a demonstration. The incident took place at D-Chowk, a high-security area in the Pakistani capital. The car was being controlled remotely over the internet when a sudden connectivity failure caused its steering to malfunction. Footage of the incident went viral and sparked a wave of memes online.

Article Title: Pak PM scrambles for damage control after his office edits leaders out of SCO summit photo
Article Text:
The edited framing keeps Sharif at the centre alongside several prominent leaders

What’s was on the agenda

What

PM Modi

told SCO summit

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif appeared to go into damage-control mode on Tuesday after his office shared an edited version of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit’s family photograph, cropping out several world leaders while keeping Sharif prominently at the centre of the frame.The Pakistan Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) first shared the edited summit photograph at 11:42am IST.The full image showed the heads of SCO member states and senior officials standing together ahead of a session of the 26th SCO Summit in Bishkek.From left, the photograph featured SCO Secretary-General Nurlan Yermekbayev, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and SCO Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure chief Ularbek Sharsheev.The selective framing put Sharif at the centre of the image alongside several prominent leaders.At 3.32pm IST, the Pakistani Prime Minister shared the full family photograph featuring all the world leaders.The 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Leadership Summit focused on strengthening regional cooperation and addressing shared security, economic and geopolitical challenges.The summit, marking the SCO’s 25th anniversary was held in the expanded “SCO Plus” format, bringing together leaders from member, partner and observer countries to discuss wider regional and global issuesDuring the summit, PM Modi addressed the SCO summit and called for a united fight against terrorism, saying there could be no “double standards” on the issue.“We must dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorism--its financing, recruitment, radicalisation, and safe havens,” Modi said, adding that countries which use terrorism as an instrument of policy and provide shelter or support to terrorists must be sent a strong message.PM Modi also called for greater regional cooperation on security, connectivity and economic opportunities, while stressing dialogue and diplomacy as the way forward in addressing conflicts.
Article Summary: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif appeared to go into damage-control mode on Tuesday. His office shared an edited version of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit’s family photograph, cropping out several world leaders. The selective framing put Sharif at the centre of the image alongside several prominent leaders.

Article Title: 100-year-old Hindu temple demolished in Pakistan’s Punjab
Article Text:
PMMP chairman Aslam Parvez Sahotra said he met Punjab Additional Home Secretary on August 28 and submitted a written application seeking action against those allegedly responsible for the demolition, as well as officials accused of failing to protect the property.

Poll Vote & Share your view What steps should be prioritized to protect religious heritage sites? Stronger security and monitoring Government protection and restoration Community engagement and awareness programs 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A more than 100-year-old Hindu temple in Pakistan ’s Punjab province was demolished on August 21 in Siraj village of Narowal, around 130 km from Lahore, with minority groups alleging that religious zealots targeted the site to absorb its land into an adjacent madrassa. The government, however, has maintained that the temple collapsed because of torrential rains.The demolition has triggered demands for an investigation and restoration of the temple, with the Pakistan Masiha Millat Party (PMMP) accusing local authorities and the Evacuee Trust Property Board (ETPB) of failing to protect the centuries-old Hindu place of worship.PMMP chairman Aslam Parvez Sahotra said he met Punjab Additional Home Secretary on August 28 and submitted a written application seeking action against those allegedly responsible for the demolition, as well as officials accused of failing to protect the property.Sahotra alleged that the people involved in the demolition were associated with the Tehreek-i-Labbaik Pakistan (TLP), a banned far-right Islamic party. He further claimed that after the temple was brought down, metal fittings from its shikhar, bricks and other material were removed from the site.The temple, estimated to be between 100 and 125 years old, stood on approximately 1,000 square metres of land in Siraj village.The dispute over the site predates its demolition. According to Sahotra, land adjoining the temple had earlier been leased by the ETPB for a madrassa. The lease was subsequently cancelled after rent allegedly went unpaid for several years and the premises were not used for the stated purpose.He said several people later occupied portions of the property illegally.Sahotra referred to a revenue department report which identified individuals as illegal occupants of the temple’s quarters and other parts of the property. He said the ETPB deputy administrator in Sialkot cancelled the seminary’s lease rights on January 29, 2026, and ordered the eviction of illegal occupants and sealing of the property.“This order was not implemented,” Sahotra alleged.A report attributed to the DSP Narowal, dated April 11, also indicated that local police were aware of security concerns surrounding the temple and the possibility that it could be damaged, according to Sahotra.The ETPB, however, has rejected the allegation that the temple was deliberately demolished.ETPB senior official Rana Iftikhar told PTI that the temple had collapsed following torrential rains. He acknowledged its historical significance, saying, “The temple carries no name in our record books. However, it is a very old one... more than 100 to 125 years old,” he said.Iftikhar also confirmed that the land adjoining the temple had been leased for a seminary, but maintained that the temple's own land had not been leased.“However, the temple's land is not given to anyone for lease,” he said and added the ETPB highups will decide about restoration of the temple.The conflicting accounts have heightened concerns among members of the local Hindu community.Hindu community leader Rattan Lal condemned the demolition and called for the government to order the temple's restoration. He said the district administration and ETPB had failed to take adequate steps to secure the site or remove alleged illegal occupants.“The district administration and the ETPB failed to take adequate measures to protect the site or remove the alleged occupants, ultimately allowing the temple to be demolished,” Lal said and asked the government to take action against those found involved in the demolition of the temple.Lal, who is also a Hindu member of the Narowal District Peace Committee and the Pak Dharam Astan Hindu Committee, said members of the community were now reluctant to approach the site.“We are even afraid to visit the site because of the madrassa that continues to operate on its premises.”Sahotra has called for the temple to be rebuilt in its original form and urged the Punjab government to strengthen protection for Hindu temples, Sikh gurdwaras and Christian churches, along with their adjoining properties.Arya, meanwhile, said decades of conflict between Pakistan and India, the Islamisation policies of the 1980s and the 1992 demolition of the Babri Masjid in India had contributed to a sense of insecurity among local Hindus.“Preserving Hindu heritage can improve the image of Pakistan and attract tourism.”
Article Summary: More than 100-year-old Hindu temple in Pakistan's Punjab province was demolished on August 21. Minority groups claim the temple was demolished to make way for an Islamic madrassa. The Pakistan Masiha Millat Party (PMMP) has submitted a written application seeking action against those allegedly responsible.

Article Title: Lahore inflation squeezes household budgets as food, rent and utility costs rise
Article Text:
People walk through a market to shop for grocery and other items

Vegetable, LPG prices add to public anger

Rising inflation in Pakistan's Lahore has intensified financial pressures on ordinary citizens, with soaring prices of food, rent, utilities and other essentials making it increasingly difficult for low-income families to make ends meet, new agency ANI reported.Residents said the rising cost of basic commodities has made it difficult for some households to afford even two meals a day. Prices of flour, cooking oil, pulses, vegetables and other necessities have continued to rise, while daily-wage workers and low-income earners said their incomes have failed to keep pace with inflation.Citizens also raised concerns over sharply higher vegetable prices, saying commonly consumed items such as potatoes and tomatoes have become increasingly unaffordable. Residents said vegetables were being sold for around Rs 150 to Rs 300 per kilogram, depending on the item and market.One resident appealed to the government to address the difficulties faced by poor families, saying rising food prices, rent and utility bills had made household management extremely challenging. Families on limited incomes, he said, were increasingly being forced to choose between food, rent, medicines and other essential expenses.ANI reports that people living on modest pensions were struggling to manage household expenses, particularly when they also had children, medical costs and other financial responsibilities.Residents also criticised the government over LPG prices, alleging that the fuel was being sold above official rates in some markets. They questioned who would regulate traders and ensure enforcement of government price controls.Rickshaw driver Usman Ali said rising fuel and essential commodity prices had severely affected his livelihood, leaving little or nothing to save after meeting basic household expenses.Citizens further questioned why lower petrol prices had not resulted in cheaper food and other essential commodities, asking why reductions in fuel costs were not being reflected in market prices.
Article Summary: Rising prices of food, rent, utilities and other essentials making it increasingly difficult for low-income families to make ends meet. Prices of flour, cooking oil, pulses, vegetables and other necessities have continued to rise. Citizens also raised concerns over sharply higher vegetable prices. Residents also criticised the government over LPG prices.

Article Title: Kabul, Kashmir, Mumbai, Pahalgam: Hafiz Saeed’s deadly four-decade terror trail
Article Text:
Four decades of Lashkar: How Hafiz Saeed’s network moved from Afghanistan to Kashmir (Associated press image)

LeT's major attacks

The Afghan war that created LeT's foundations

Deadly Embrace: Pakistan, America, and the Future of the Global Jihad

Why Lashkar-e-Taiba was established

From Kunar to Kashmir

Lashkar-e-Taiba: From 9/11 to Mumbai

Who is Hafiz Saeed

Hafiz Saeed - From cleric to terrorist

LeT survives Pakistani ban after 9/11

Four decades of evolution

From Kashmir insurgency to Mumbai

Why Afghanistan remained part of the network

Saeed's legal history and the Pahalgam case

From Afghan jihad to Kashmir

From Afghan jihad to Pahalgam

The legal case against Lashkar-e-Taiba founder Hafiz Muhammad Saeed has acquired a fresh dimension in India. In July 2026, the National Investigation Agency named Saeed in a supplementary chargesheet in the Pahalgam terror attack case, charging him in his individual capacity and as the founder and chief of Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and its active proxy, The Resistance Front (TRF). The NIA mentioned a cross-border conspiracy behind the April 22, 2025 attack, which killed 26 civilians. A special NIA court subsequently issued a non-bailable warrant against Saeed.The development came as Mumbai Police separately began proceedings for a trial in absentia against Saeed and five other Pakistan-based accused in the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks. The proclamation covers Saeed, LeT operations chief Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, Sajid Mir, Abu Alqama, Asim alias Abu Qahafa and Major Abdur Rehman Pasha. The police have also approached the Union home ministry to facilitate service of the proclamation orders through Interpol.The two cases, separated by 17 years, bring together different phases of LeT's history. One concerns an attack in Kashmir, the region that became the organisation's principal battlefield in the 1990s. The other concerns the Mumbai attacks, which demonstrated how far LeT's operational reach had expanded beyond the Kashmir insurgency.But LeT did not begin in Kashmir, nor did Hafiz Saeed first emerge as a militant leader there. The organisation's institutional roots can be traced to the Afghan jihad of the 1980s, when Pakistan became a major centre for the mobilisation, training and movement of Islamist fighters.The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 created an environment in which Islamist networks from Pakistan and other parts of the Muslim world expanded rapidly. Among the prominent figures associated with this mobilisation was Palestinian scholar Abdullah Azzam, who helped organise foreign volunteers for the Afghan jihad and promoted the idea of jihad as a broader obligation extending beyond a single battlefield.It was in this environment that Azzam worked with Hafiz Saeed, a Pakistani Sunni scholar who had studied in Saudi Arabia. According to Bruce Riedel's, the two were involved in establishing Markaz-ud-Dawa-wal-Irshad (MDI), a religious organisation that combined missionary activity with support for jihad. MDI developed training infrastructure in Afghanistan, including in Kunar province, where recruits could gain battlefield experience. Riedel also records links between the organisation and Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI).Lashkar-e-Taiba subsequently emerged as the military wing associated with this network. The US state department describes LeT as having formed in the late 1980s as the militant wing of MDI, an organisation originally established in opposition to the Soviet presence in Afghanistan. The Australian government dates LeT's formation as a military organisation to 1989.The exact formation date therefore varies depending on whether the establishment of MDI, the creation of its military wing or the later formalisation of LeT is being referred to. What is clearer is the sequence: the Afghan jihad provided the organisation's early ideological, human and training infrastructure, while the end of the Soviet war opened the way for that infrastructure to be redirected towards other conflicts.LeT's early purpose was shaped by two connected objectives: participation in the Afghan jihad and preparation for jihad in Kashmir and India. Riedel describes MDI's objective as applying the experience of the Afghan war to Kashmir and India, including training Kashmiris alongside Afghan mujahideen so they could gain combat experience.The changing situation in Afghanistan accelerated that transition. The Soviet withdrawal meant that the battlefield that had brought together thousands of militants was no longer the same. At the same time, violence in Jammu and Kashmir was rising sharply.The Australian government's account of LeT's history says the organisation was originally formed to wage militant jihad against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan and shifted its focus to the insurgency in Indian-administered Kashmir during the 1990s after Soviet troops withdrew. It identifies the organisation's stated objective as uniting Kashmir with Pakistan, while noting that its broader ideological objectives extended beyond Kashmir.Kashmir thus became the next major theatre in which the organisation could deploy the personnel, training and networks developed during the Afghan war.The shift towards Kashmir coincided with the rapid growth of the insurgency there. Riedel records that incidents of violence in Kashmir rose from 390 in 1988 to 2,100 in 1989 and nearly 4,000 in 1990. Against this backdrop, Saeed's organisation began establishing infrastructure in and around Kashmir while maintaining training facilities in Pakistan and Afghanistan.LeT's emergence also coincided with changes among the various groups fighting in Kashmir. The Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front advocated an independent Kashmir, while Pakistan's security establishment increasingly favoured groups committed to the territory's integration with Pakistan. Riedel describes efforts to strengthen pro-Pakistan organisations and isolate the JKLF, which was regarded as too independent. Hizbul Mujahideen became a major pro-Pakistan militant force, while LeT developed its own network and capabilities.By the 1990s, Kashmir had become LeT's principal operational theatre. The organisation developed training and recruitment networks and directed fighters towards attacks on Indian security forces. Stephen Tankel, in, describes Kashmir as the group's primary objective even as its connections to the wider global jihadist movement expanded.This distinction is important. LeT developed relationships with al Qaida and other jihadist groups, but its core focus remained India and Kashmir. Riedel similarly distinguishes between the different objectives of the groups operating in the region, noting that the Afghan Taliban remained primarily focused on Afghanistan while LeT concentrated on South Asia. At the operational level, however, their cooperation increased.Saeed's prominence grew alongside the institutional development of MDI and LeT. He was not simply the leader of an armed organisation. The network around him combined religious propagation, education, charity and terror activity.Riedel describes Saeed as a prominent Pakistani Sunni scholar who worked with Azzam in developing MDI. The organisation's combination of religious activity and military infrastructure provided the foundation for the later growth of LeT.LeT's recruitment base was also closely connected to Pakistani society. Riedel writes that the organisation was predominantly Punjabi and recruited from many of the same communities and neighbourhoods as the Pakistani army and ISI. He also describes LeT camps located near army bases and the involvement of retired military personnel in training fighters.The nature and extent of state support for LeT has remained a matter of dispute, but the organisation's relationship with Pakistan's security establishment became an important part of its history. The United Nations Security Council identifies LeT as a Pakistan-based organisation and records its links with al Qaida and the Taliban, as well as its use of Jamaat-ud-Dawa for financial, logistical and infrastructural support.The September 11, 2001 attacks changed the environment for militant organisations operating from Pakistan. The United States designated LeT as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation in December 2001, while Pakistan banned the group in January 2002.The ban, however, did not eliminate the network. The US state department says Saeed subsequently changed the group's name to Jamaat-ud-Dawa and expanded its humanitarian activities, while continuing to disseminate its message through JuD's media outlets.Riedel similarly writes that although LeT was formally banned, it continued to operate and Saeed remained in charge. He describes the organisation's large facility at Muridke near Lahore, which included schools, dormitories, a garment factory, an iron foundry and a mosque.This structure helped the network maintain a presence beyond its armed operations. Religious institutions, charitable activity, fundraising and recruitment provided a broader organisational base that could continue even when the LeT name itself faced restrictions.The United Nations says LeT used JuD as a front through which it provided financial, logistical and infrastructural support for terrorist activity. It also records that an al Qaida operative, Abu Zubaydah, was captured in 2002 in a LeT safe house in Faisalabad, illustrating the organisation's connections to the wider jihadist network.The years after 2001 saw LeT's operational reach extend beyond the traditional Kashmir battlefield. The United Nations records that the organisation conducted terrorist operations against military and civilian targets from the 1990s onwards, including attacks in New Delhi and Mumbai and the December 2001 Parliament attack, in which Jaish-e-Mohammed was also involved.The 2008 Mumbai attacks represented the most significant expansion of that reach. Ten attackers carried out coordinated assaults across Mumbai between November 26 and 29, killing 166 people. The attack targeted several locations, including the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi-Trident and Nariman House.The operation also demonstrated the organisational depth behind LeT's attacks. Riedel's account details the role of David Coleman Headley, who joined LeT in Pakistan and later conducted reconnaissance in Mumbai. Between 2005 and 2008, Headley travelled repeatedly to India, studying targets, recording locations and reporting back to LeT.The Mumbai operation therefore represented more than an extension of the Kashmir insurgency. It demonstrated the organisation's ability to plan and execute a complex attack far from its traditional theatre while drawing on personnel, training and logistical networks developed over decades.The shift to Kashmir did not end LeT's involvement in Afghanistan. Instead, the two theatres became connected through overlapping militant networks.Riedel wrote that LeT became increasingly active in Afghanistan, including operations against Indian interests and clashes with Nato forces. He also described growing operational links between LeT and the Afghan Taliban, particularly the Haqqani network.The United Nations likewise records LeT's activity in Afghanistan and its links with al Qaida and the Taliban. The Australian government has documented LeT's continued presence in Afghanistan and reported that the UN estimated the group had close to 1,000 members operating there in May 2020.Afghanistan therefore remained an important part of LeT's network even after Kashmir became its main operational focus. The relationships, training environments and infrastructure developed during the Afghan jihad continued to provide connections to other militant organisations.Saeed's subsequent legal history illustrates the difference between Pakistan's formal action against LeT and the organisation's continued existence through associated structures.Pakistan arrested Saeed in 2019 on terrorism-financing charges. He was convicted in several cases and received additional sentences in subsequent proceedings. The UN Security Council's current sanctions information says Saeed is in Pakistani custody serving a cumulative 78-year sentence following convictions in seven terrorism-financing cases.India, meanwhile, has continued to pursue him over alleged involvement in major terror attacks attributed to LeT.The latest development is the NIA's supplementary chargesheet in the Pahalgam case. The agency has named Saeed both individually and as the chief of LeT and TRF, alleging that he was part of the wider conspiracy behind the April 2025 attack.The subsequent non-bailable warrant followed the NIA's request for Saeed's arrest and custodial interrogation. Meanwhile, Mumbai Police has begun the process for an in-absentia trial against Saeed and five other Pakistan-based accused in the 26/11 case.Lashkar-e-Taiba's four-decade history can be traced through a sequence of changing battlefields and organisational forms. Its foundations were laid during the Afghan jihad, when Hafiz Saeed and Abdullah Azzam helped build MDI and the networks around it. After the Soviet withdrawal, the organisation redirected much of its experience and infrastructure towards Kashmir, where it became a major Pakistan-based militant group.The 2002 ban did not erase the network. It adapted through Jamaat-ud-Dawa and other associated structures, while maintaining religious, charitable and recruitment networks across Pakistan. Its links with militant groups operating in Afghanistan also survived, even as India and Kashmir remained its central focus.The Mumbai attacks showed how far that network could project violence beyond Kashmir. The Pahalgam investigation has now brought the story back to the same region where LeT established much of its early operational identity.The latest legal proceedings against Saeed therefore sit at the end of a history that began not in Mumbai or Pahalgam, but in the Afghan jihad of the 1980s.
Article Summary: The legal case against Hafiz Muhammad Saeed has acquired a fresh dimension in India.
